title: Spotify tracks
text:
Provenance and license
Collected from the Spotify Web API by Kaylin Pavlik (January 2020) and published as the TidyTuesday dataset of 21 January 2020, 32,833 rows. Spotify’s developer terms restrict commercial use; this is teaching. The course file is 10,000 tracks drawn at random from the 28,356 distinct tracks.


R access
readr::read_csv("https://ml4ds.com/files/spotify_tracks.csv"), then one row per track_id (the loader below).


Unit of observation
A track. The file has a row per track and playlist (11,554 rows), since 1,101 tracks are in more than one playlist. Columns: track_id, track_name, track_artist, track_popularity (0 to 100), release_date, release_year, playlist_genre, playlist_subgenre, and the audio features danceability, energy, key, loudness, mode, speechiness, acousticness, instrumentalness, liveness, valence, tempo, duration_ms.


Target and loss
track_popularity with squared error. Variance about 560; a tenth of the tracks score exactly 0.


Available at prediction time
The audio features and the release date are properties of the recording. The genre is the playlist’s, not the track’s. Popularity is Spotify’s score in January 2020 and rewards recent plays, so release_year carries recency as well as era.


Permitted predictors
Week 5: the ten audio features (duration_ms in minutes), release_year and playlist_genre.


Missingness
None in the features; one track lacks a name.


Split unit and seed
Tracks, with set.seed(5): 5,000 training, 2,000 selection, 3,000 test. A split by row puts the same track on both sides (a leakage example for later in the course).


Baseline
The training mean, 39.1: MSE 581 on the selection tracks, where least squares on the eleven numeric inputs scores about 541 and \(k\) nearest neighbors on the same inputs about 528. The test scores are the seminar’s.


Methods that use it
Week 5: the lecture’s demonstrations and the seminar’s leaderboard. Later: cross-validation and the leakage check.


Complication it carries
The score is a snapshot of plays, not a judgment of the music; the playlists were one person’s choice in one month.


Limitations
Six genres, no lyrics, no artist history, no play counts. Fine for the mechanism, not for a claim about music.


Fictional?
No.

title: Spotify tracks
text:
Loader
library(tidyverse)
sp <- read_csv("https://ml4ds.com/files/spotify_tracks.csv") |>
  distinct(track_id, .keep_all = TRUE) |>          # one row per track
  mutate(duration_min = duration_ms / 60000, genre = factor(playlist_genre))

title: Movies
text:
Provenance and licence
The IMDb data extracted by Hadley Wickham for the ggplot2 package’s original movies dataset and moved to the ggplot2movies package. Its documentation says films were included if they had a known length and at least one user rating; the shipped data run to 2005 and every film has at least five votes (the documentation’s row count, 28,819, is stale against the 58,788 shipped). GPL-3 for the package (packageDescription("ggplot2movies")$License). IMDb’s own terms restrict commercial use of its data; this is teaching.


R access
ggplot2movies::movies (package version 0.0.1).


Unit of observation
A film (58,788 rows), 24 columns: title, year (1893–2005), length (minutes), budget (91% missing), rating (average user rating, 1–10), votes, r1 to r10 (the share of users giving each rating, coarsened), mpaa (blank for 92% of films), and seven genre indicators (Action, Animation, Comedy, Drama, Documentary, Romance, Short).


Target and loss
rating with squared error.


Available at prediction time
year, length, the genre indicators. votes and the r1–r10 columns come from the same users’ ratings and are not honest predictors of rating (the r columns nearly determine it). budget is mostly missing.


Permitted predictors
Weeks 5 and 8 use length and year only, as smooth terms. Genre indicators may be added as linear terms in mgcv (+ Comedy + Drama).


Missingness
budget 91% missing and unused; nothing else.


Selection
The course filters to length <= 200, length > 10, year > 1918, votes >= 5 (the last removes nothing): 53,388 films. The 4,805 films of ten minutes or less are shorts, the 250 above 200 minutes are serials and epics, and the 630 films from before 1919 are sparse; each group would dominate the ends of a length or year curve.


Split unit
Films. No seed in the seminar notebook, so a random 70/30 split and a subsample of 5,000 for the by-hand loop differ across students. The split in time (train before 1990, test from 1990 on) is deterministic: 31,412 and 21,976 films. It is a retrospective check using one snapshot of ratings, not a forecast made in 1990.


Baseline
Predict the mean rating (5.88): mean squared error 2.43 (the variance of rating). The additive model on length and year reaches about 2.15 on a random split, and 3.16 on the split in time, worse than the training mean (2.66).


Methods that use it
Week 5: the additive model as least squares on spline basis functions, lm(rating ~ ns(length, 8) + ns(year, 8)), and its component plots. Week 8: the separate smooth against the backfitted component; mgcv; backfitting by hand on a subsample; the two splits. The legacy GAM deck and notebook used the same data.


Complication it carries
Ratings come from people who chose to watch a film and then to rate it. Films of 60 to 80 minutes are mostly old (median year 1956), and older films here are rated higher; one plausible explanation is that the old films still watched are the ones that survived, but the association does not identify that, and cohort and genre are other explanations the data cannot separate. The split in time shows a second complication: films from 1990 on have years the training data never contained, so the year component is evaluated outside its data.


Limitations
Ratings up to 2005 from a site whose users were not a sample of anyone; length as reported to IMDb; no director, cast, language or country. Fine for the mechanism of additive fitting and for the two splits, not for a claim about films.


Fictional?
No.

title: Machine learning
text:
Where week 3 left the fitting
Week 2: least squares has a formula for \(\hat\beta\), and \(\hat\beta\) solves the normal equations. Week 3: logistic regression is fitted by maximum likelihood, and glm did it for us
Today’s question, in three parts: what did glm do? how can we tell whether fitting is working? should we let it finish?

Write down the normal equations from memory. Then guess: how is it different for logistic regression?

title: Machine learning
text:
Model fitting: maximum likelihood
How do we estimate \(\beta\)? Maximum likelihood:
\[
\text{maximize } L(\beta ; \mathbf y | \mathbf X) = \prod_{i=1}^n L(\beta ; y_i | \mathbf x_i)
\] (assuming the data is i.i.d.)

Maximum likelihood (Fisher, 1912–1922): choose the parameter that makes the observed data most probable. We maximize the log-likelihood because a product of \(n\) small numbers underflows and a sum differentiates term by term; log is increasing, so the maximizer is the same. Least squares is a log-likelihood: for \(y_i \sim N(\mathbf x_i^T\beta, \sigma^2)\) it is \(-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_i (y_i - \mathbf x_i^T\beta)^2 + \text{const}\). In glm, family names the distribution whose likelihood is maximized: gaussian is lm, binomial is logistic regression.

Next slide: a bit of mathematics

title: Machine learning
text:
MLE for logistic regression
Each factor is a Bernoulli (binomial, one trial) probability, \(P(y_i \mid \mathbf x_i) = p_i^{y_i}(1 - p_i)^{1 - y_i}\) with \(p_i = p(\mathbf x_i^T\beta) = 1/(1 + e^{-\mathbf x_i^T\beta})\):
\[
L(\beta ; \mathbf y | \mathbf X) = \prod_{i=1}^n \left( \frac{1}{1+e^{-\mathbf x_i^T\beta}} \right)^{y_i} \left(1- \frac{1}{1+e^{-\mathbf x_i^T\beta}} \right)^{1-y_i}
\]

\[
\ell(\beta ; \mathbf y | \mathbf X) = \sum_{i=1}^n \left[ y_i \log \left( \frac{1}{1+e^{-\mathbf x_i^T\beta}} \right) + (1-y_i) \log \left(1- \frac{1}{1+e^{- \mathbf x_i^T\beta}} \right) \right]
\]

title: Machine learning
text:
MLE: the derivative
\[
\frac{\partial}{\partial \beta} \ell(\beta ; \mathbf y | \mathbf X) = \sum_{i=1}^n \left[ y_i  \left( \frac{\mathbf x_i e^{-\mathbf x_i^T\beta}}{1+e^{-\mathbf x_i^T\beta}} \right) + (1-y_i) \left(\frac{-\mathbf x_i}{1+e^{- \mathbf x_i^T\beta}} \right) \right]
\]
\[= \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbf x_i \left[ y_i - \left(\frac{1}{1+e^{- \mathbf x_i^T\beta}} \right) \right] = \color{#b73779}{\sum_{i=1}^n \mathbf x_i [y_i - \hat p_i(\beta)]}\]
Set this equal to 0 and solve for \(\beta\). How: the rest of today

title: Machine learning
section: The score equations, read as orthogonality
text:
The score equations, read as orthogonality

Week 2, least squares: \(\mathbf X^T(\mathbf y - \mathbf X\hat\beta) = \mathbf 0\). The residual is orthogonal to every column of \(\mathbf X\).

Logistic score equations. Stack the last slide’s rows: writing \(\mathbf p(\beta) = (\hat p_1(\beta), \ldots, \hat p_n(\beta))^T\), the MLE \(\hat\beta\) solves \[
\mathbf X^T\big(\mathbf y - \mathbf p(\hat\beta)\big) = \mathbf 0
\]
Same shape as least squares, with \(\mathbf X\hat\beta\) replaced by the fitted probabilities: the residual \(\mathbf y - \hat{\mathbf p}\) is orthogonal to every column of \(\mathbf X\)
No closed form, because \(\mathbf p(\beta)\) is not linear in \(\beta\)

title: Machine learning
section: Two things the score equations say
text:
Two things the score equations say
Row one is the intercept. \(\sum_i (y_i - \hat p_i) = 0\): the fitted probabilities average to the observed proportion of 1s on the training rows.
The log-likelihood is concave. Differentiating once more, \[
\frac{\partial^2 \ell}{\partial\beta\,\partial\beta^T} = -\sum_{i=1}^n w_i\, \mathbf x_i\mathbf x_i^T, \qquad w_i = \hat p_i(\beta)\,\big(1 - \hat p_i(\beta)\big) > 0
\] Each term is \(-w_i\, \mathbf x_i\mathbf x_i^T\) with \(w_i > 0\). In any direction \(v\), \(v^T \mathbf x_i\mathbf x_i^T v = (\mathbf x_i^T v)^2 \ge 0\), so the sum curves downward, or is flat, in every direction: the log-likelihood is concave, and any finite solution of the score equations is its global maximum
What concavity does not give: existence (week 3’s separable case has no finite solution). So how do we solve the score equations?

text:
Newton-Raphson

Find the roots of a function
Iteratively approximating the function by its tangent
Root of the tangent line is used as starting point for next approximation
See the animation on Wikipedia

Exercise: using the gradient and the Hessian from the previous slides, derive the Newton-Raphson update for \(\beta\)

title: Machine learning
text:
Logistic regression fitting: multivariate case
Newton-IRLS (equivalent) steps, \(g\) the logit link. The one line to keep: each iteration is a weighted least-squares fit around the current fit
\[
\begin{eqnarray}
\hat{\mathbf p}_t & \gets & g^{-1}(\mathbf X \hat \beta_t)
& \ \text{ update probs.} \\
\mathbf W_t & \gets & \text{diag}[\hat{\mathbf p}_t (1 - \hat{\mathbf p}_t)]
& \ \text{ update weights} \\
\hat{\mathbf{y}}_t & \gets & g(\hat{\mathbf p}_t) + \mathbf W_t^{-1}(\mathbf y - \hat{\mathbf p}_t)
& \ \text{ update response}
\end{eqnarray}
\]
and then update parameter estimate (LS sub-problem) \[\hat{\beta}_{t+1} \gets \arg \min_{\beta} (\hat{\mathbf{y}}_t - \mathbf X \beta)^T \mathbf W_t (\hat{\mathbf{y}}_t - \mathbf X \beta)\]

Note: larger weights on observations with \(\hat p\) closer to 1/2, i.e. the most difficult to classify (look for variations of this theme) See Section 4.4.1 of ESL

title: Machine learning
section: GLMs in R: what you should know
text:
GLMs in R: what you should know
Does glm use Newton-Raphson for every family? Its fitter is IRLS, which is Fisher scoring: Newton with the expected Hessian in place of the actual one. For the default links (binomial-logit, poisson-log, gaussian-identity) the two coincide; for other links it is a close relative. lm is the one-step case
How many iterations? Usually under ten. summary() prints Number of Fisher Scoring iterations
When does it fail? Mostly when there is no finite MLE, week 3’s separable case, with coefficients growing at every iteration. The warning fitted probabilities numerically 0 or 1 occurred is a symptom to investigate, not a diagnosis: a finite MLE with a steep slope triggers it too
Why does the rest of machine learning not do this? Each step solves a \(p \times p\) system. For \(p\) in the millions that is the cost that matters; the next part avoids it

title: Machine learning
text:
Part 2: gradient descent
ML \(\approx\) ERM \(+\) SGD

title: Machine learning
text:
ML tasks as optimization problems
For a given loss function \(\ell(y, f(x))\) and probability model \((X,Y) \sim P\), we want to find a function \(f\) to minimize risk:
\[
\underset{f}{\text{minimize }}\ R(f) = \mathbb E_P[\ell(Y, f(X))]
\]

Math model \(\leftrightarrow\) Statistical model
Assume an i.i.d. sample from \(P\), focus on empirical risk minimization (ERM)
\[
\underset{f \in \mathcal F}{\text{minimize }}\ \hat R_n(f) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \ell(y_i, f(x_i))
\]

We also choose a function class \(\mathcal F\) (or parameter set), i.e. a class of functions \(f\), determining the domain of the optimization

title: Machine learning
text:
Examples: linear regression, GLM
Linear regression. Probability model: errors \(\varepsilon \sim N(0, \sigma^2)\). Loss: squared, \(\ell(y, f(\mathbf x)) = (y - f(\mathbf x))^2\). Class: \(\mathcal F = \{ f_\beta(\mathbf x) = \mathbf x^T \beta : \beta \in \mathbb R^{p+1} \}\). Algorithm: OLS, closed form (memorized yet?) \[\underset{\beta \in \mathbb R^{p+1}}{\text{minimize }} \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \mathbf x_i^T \beta)^2\]

GLM. Probability model: family = binomial(), poisson(), etc. Loss: negative log-likelihood, so \(\hat R_n(\beta) = -\ell(\beta)/n\). Class: \(\{ g^{-1}(\mathbf x^T \beta) : \beta \in \mathbb R^{p+1} \}\), link \(g\) fixed. Algorithm: ERM (here also MLE), usually by an iterative algorithm \[
\underset{\beta \in \mathbb R^{p+1}}{\text{minimize }} -\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \log L(\beta ; y_i | \mathbf x_i)
\]

title: Machine learning
text:
(Iterative) optimization algorithms
Downside of Newton-Raphson: requires second derivatives, including inverting the \(p \times p\) Hessian matrix when optimizing over \(p > 1\) parameters
If \(p\) is large, second-order optimization methods like Newton’s are very costly

First order methods only require computing the \(p \times 1\) gradient vector
Recall that the gradient is a vector in the direction of steepest increase in the parameter space

title: Machine learning
text:
Gradient (steepest) descent
i.e. skiing as fast as possible. Notation: the objective is the empirical risk \(\hat R_n(\beta)\), and \(t\) counts steps

Start at an initial point \(\beta_0\)
For step \(t = 1, \ldots\)

Compute \(\mathbf d_t = \nabla \hat R_n(\beta_{t-1}) \color{#b73779}{\text{ (gradient)}}\)
Update \(\beta_{t} = \beta_{t-1} - \gamma_t \mathbf d_t\)

Until some convergence criteria is satisfied


Where the step size \(\gamma_t > 0\) is made small enough to not “overshoot” and increase the loss, i.e. the loss only decreases

title: Machine learning
text:
Which step size?












The valley: \(f(\beta) = \tfrac12(\beta_1^2 + 10\beta_2^2)\), ten times steeper across than along. Gradient descent from the orange point, \(\gamma = 0.15\)
A few zigzags across, then a crawl along


The valley, same start, three step sizes: \(\gamma = 0.05\), \(\gamma = 0.18\), \(\gamma = 0.21\). For each, commit: converges, converges slowly, or diverges?

title: Machine learning
text:
Three step sizes


































Across the valley the update multiplies \(\beta_2\) by \(1 - 10\gamma\): \(0.5\), \(-0.8\), \(-1.1\)
The largest curvature sets the largest safe step; the smallest sets how long it takes

title: Machine learning
text:
The quadratic case, exactly
One direction with curvature \(a > 0\): \(f(\beta) = \tfrac12 a\beta^2\), \(\nabla f = a\beta\), so
\[
\beta_{t+1} = \beta_t - \gamma a\beta_t = (1 - \gamma a)\,\beta_t, \qquad \beta_t = (1 - \gamma a)^t \beta_0
\]
Converges iff \(|1 - \gamma a| < 1\), i.e. \(0 < \gamma < 2/a\). The step \(\gamma = 1/a\) lands in one move

Several directions with curvatures \(a_1 \ge \dots \ge a_d > 0\), one step size for all of them: \(\gamma < 2/a_1\) to converge, and the slowest direction shrinks like \(\max_j |1 - \gamma a_j|^t\), which for \(\gamma \le 1/a_1\) is \((1 - \gamma a_d)^t\)

The largest curvature sets the safe step; the ratio \(a_1/a_d\), the shape of the valley, sets the speed (a direction with \(a_j = 0\), as in least squares with \(p > n\), never moves). For least squares, \(\hat R_n(\beta) = \frac1n\|\mathbf y - \mathbf X\beta\|^2\), the \(a_j\) are the eigenvalues of \(2\mathbf X^T\mathbf X/n\)

text: Part 3: gradient diagnostics

title: Machine learning
text:
Reading the gradient










Your loss has stopped falling. Which of the four places are you at, and how would you tell?

title: Machine learning
text:
Landscapes










The saddle: compute the gradient at \((0, 0)\); is it a minimum? One of the three starts is \((0, 1.2)\): where does its path end, and why does it never leave?

Where you start decides where you end. Least squares and logistic regression have one valley (convex); most of what comes after week 7 does not

title: Machine learning
text:
Too big, too small









Too big a step (\(\gamma = 12 > 2/L = 8\)): overshoot and bounce. Too small a gradient (the plateau, \(0.01\)): creep for hundreds of steps, then move all at once. In deep networks the chain rule can make gradients explode or vanish

title: Machine learning
text:
Has it converged?










Three runs, 200 steps, log scales. One has converged, one is on a plateau, one has a step size that shrank to nothing. Which is which?

title: Machine learning
section: Has it converged? The next 600 steps
text:
Has it converged? The next 600 steps










A, the valley: converged. B, the hilly road: its loss fell by 0.005 in 200 steps, its gradient is \(0.01\) and not shrinking; the drop comes at step 445. C, the valley with steps \(0.3 \cdot 0.6^t\): stopped short

title: Machine learning
text:
Directions with zero slope
These are some of the issues that make optimization hard. What’s more: in \(\mathbb R^d\) the slope is zero in \(d - 1\) directions; whether they lead down is a question of curvature










The gradient is zero. What else would tell you a minimum from a saddle?

title: Machine learning
text:
Curvature

Taylor, to second order, with \(H = \nabla^2 f(x)\) the Hessian: for a smooth \(f\) and a small move \(\delta\), \(f(x + \delta) \approx f(x) + \nabla f(x)^T\delta + \tfrac12\,\delta^T H\,\delta\).

What decides whether a step helps is how fast the gradient changes along it. Take the step \(\delta = -\gamma\nabla f(x)\): \[
f(x - \gamma\nabla f(x)) \approx f(x) \;\underbrace{-\; \gamma\,\|\nabla f(x)\|^2}_{\text{always down}} \;\underbrace{+\; \tfrac12\gamma^2\, \nabla f(x)^T H\, \nabla f(x)}_{\text{the curvature pushes back}}
\]
In the quadratic case the curvature was a fixed number \(a\). On the saddle it is \(+8\) at the two minima and \(-4\) at the saddle point; on the hilly road’s plateau it is about \(0\)

title: Machine learning
text:
Curvature at most \(L\)
If the curvature in every direction is at most \(L\) in size, the push-back is at most \(\tfrac12 L\gamma^2\|\nabla f(x)\|^2\), and then \[
f(x - \gamma\nabla f(x)) \lesssim f(x) - \gamma\underbrace{\big(1 - \tfrac12 L\gamma\big)}_{> 0 \text{ for } \gamma < 2/L}\|\nabla f(x)\|^2
\] The bound is best at \(\gamma = 1/L\): the quadratic case’s rule, in general

To make it a theorem, say “curvature at most \(L\)” about the gradient: Assumption. \(\nabla f\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz for some \(L > 0\): \(\|\nabla f(x) - \nabla f(y)\| \le L\,\|x - y\|\) for all \(x, y\)
A quadratic with curvatures \(a_j\) has \(L = \max_j |a_j|\) (the valley: 10); least squares, \(L = 2\lambda_{\max}(\mathbf X^T\mathbf X)/n\); the saddle has no single \(L\) (curvature \(12u^2 - 4\) in \(u\))

title: Machine learning
text:
Descent lemma

Descent lemma. If \(\nabla f\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz, then for every \(x\) \[
f\!\left(x - \tfrac1L\nabla f(x)\right) \le f(x) - \frac{\|\nabla f(x)\|^2}{2L}
\] Every step of size \(1/L\) decreases \(f\) by at least the squared gradient over \(2L\) (strictly, unless \(\nabla f(x) = 0\)).

Says: each step helps, more where the gradient is large. No convexity needed
Does not say: where the steps end, or that they end

text: Part 4: stochastic gradient descent

title: Machine learning
text:
What a step costs
Second-order methods invert the \(p \times p\) Hessian; first-order methods compute the \(p \times 1\) gradient. For a linear model or a GLM, where one row’s gradient costs about \(p\) operations:









Operations
Once or per step?




Least-squares formula \((\mathbf X^T\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf X^T\mathbf y\)
about \(np^2 + p^3\)
once


One gradient-descent step
about \(np\)
per step


One step on a random batch of \(b\) rows
about \(bp\)
per step




\(n = 1{,}200{,}000\) images, \(p = 60{,}000{,}000\) parameters. If one image’s gradient cost about \(p\) operations, roughly how many is one full gradient? And one step on a batch of 128?

title: Machine learning
text:
Stochastic/random descent

Instead of computing the gradient of the loss function on the entire dataset, compute it on a random sample


Pick one row \(I\) uniformly at random from \(\{1, \ldots, n\}\) and use its gradient \(\nabla\ell_I(\beta)\) in place of the average over all \(n\) rows. Commit: is it biased for the full gradient \(\nabla\hat R_n(\beta)\), yes or no? And does the descent lemma’s guarantee carry over to a step along it?

title: Machine learning
text:
The stochastic gradient is unbiased

How would you prove this?


With the data and \(\beta\) held fixed, only \(I\) is random, and by linearity of \(\nabla\), \(\mathbb E\) and \(\sum\), \[
\mathbb E_I\big[\nabla\ell_I(\beta)\big] = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac1n\,\nabla\ell_i(\beta) = \nabla\hat R_n(\beta)
\]
Unbiased, whatever the data are. A batch of \(b\) rows drawn with replacement averages \(b\) such gradients: still unbiased
Compute update using one randomly sampled observation, or a randomly sampled subset (“mini-batch SGD”). Correct on average, cheap, and not guaranteed to decrease the training loss on any one step: the descent lemma is about the full gradient

title: Machine learning
text:
The two paths












Simulated least squares, \(n = 200\), two inputs; \(\times\) is the answer
Blue: 30 full gradient steps, \(6{,}000\) row-gradients. Orange: 600 single-row steps, \(600\) row-gradients, step \(0.05/(1 + t/100)\)
A tenth of the work, and it never sits still. The step must shrink, but not so fast that it stops short like panel C (Robbins and Monro, 1951)

title: Machine learning
text:
History: ImageNet, 2012
60,000,000
parameters in the network described in the paper, fitted in five to six days on two gaming graphics cards by stochastic gradient descent, on a loss with every feature of part 3
The winning entry, an ensemble of seven such networks, cut the ImageNet top-5 test error to 15.3%, against 26.2% for the next best. Nobody solved an equation, and no theorem said the descent would find anything good
Krizhevsky, Sutskever and Hinton, “ImageNet classification with deep convolutional neural networks”, NeurIPS 2012

title: Machine learning
text: Part 5: when to stop iterating?

title: Machine learning
text:
Early stopping
Optimization time = complexity

For many optimization algorithms the model fits closer to the training data the longer the optimization algorithm runs



e.g. the more steps of (stochastic) gradient descent used in combination with a flexible function class
e.g. the more steps of forward stepwise (adding more predictor variables)



Idea: control model complexity by stopping the algorithm before convergence
This is early stopping – we’ll come back to it later

title: Machine learning
section: Stopping early: choose a stopping point
text:
Stopping early: choose a stopping point












The wide regression: simulated least squares, \(n = 80\), \(p = 60\), noise sd 3, from \(\beta_0 = \mathbf 0\) with step \(1/2L\)
The training error, the number the algorithm sees, falls at every step and is still falling at 300

You may stop the algorithm at any step. Which one, and why?

title: Machine learning
section: Stopping early: what the training loss did not show
text:
Stopping early: what the training loss did not show












The wide regression scored on 2,000 new rows from the same model: the held-out error falls, turns at step 15, and ends far above its minimum
Every diagnostic in part 3 watched the training loss, and every one said “keep going”. Tracking the training loss is not tracking the loss you care about

title: Machine learning
section: Where the error comes from, this time
text:
Where the error comes from, this time
Three functions. \(f^\star = \arg\min_f R(f)\): the best of all (squared loss: week 2’s conditional mean). \(f_{\mathcal F} = \arg\min_{f \in \mathcal F} R(f)\): the best in the class, fixed once \(\mathcal F\) is. \(\hat f = \arg\min_{f \in \mathcal F} \hat R_n(f)\): what the data give, random
Bias–variance decomposition, ERM form. Both underbraced terms are \(\ge 0\): \[
R(\hat f) = R(f^\star) + \underbrace{\big[R(\hat f) - R(f_{\mathcal F})\big]}_{\text{estimation}} + \underbrace{\big[R(f_{\mathcal F}) - R(f^\star)\big]}_{\text{approximation}}
\]
Proof: exercise 2

title: Machine learning
text:
No free lunch
No free lunch (stated). No method has lower error than every other on every distribution. Binary classification, 0–1 loss: for any learning method and any training size \(n\), on a domain with at least \(2n\) points there is a distribution for which a perfect predictor exists and the method’s expected error (over training samples) is at least \(1/4\)
Says: choosing a method is an assumption about the world; the ERM form shows where one such assumption enters, the class \(\mathcal F\) chosen before the data
Does not say: all methods are equally good

title: Machine learning
text:
Optimal threshold theorem
Optimal threshold theorem. Let \(p(x) = P(Y = 1 \mid X = x)\), and let a false positive cost \(c_{FP}\) and a false negative \(c_{FN}\), both \(\ge 0\) and not both \(0\). The rule that minimizes expected cost at \(x\) predicts \(1\) exactly when \[
p(x) > c^\star = \frac{c_{FP}}{c_{FP} + c_{FN}},
\] and at \(p(x) = c^\star\) either prediction is optimal. Equal costs give \(c^\star = \tfrac12\): predict the more probable class, the Bayes classifier.

The model gives \(p\). The costs give \(c^\star\), and somebody chose the costs. With \(\hat p\) in place of \(p\), the rule is only as good as the estimate.

Confounders: other variables that obscure the (causal) relationship from \(X\) to \(Y\), e.g.

\(X\): treatment dose

title: Machine learning
text:
Simple models for causality
Interventions are a new type of operation we may use in probability models. Consider an intervention that changes some target variable \(T\)

Forget about the arrows pointing into \(T\) (intervention makes them irrelevant)
Change \(T\), e.g. setting it to some arbitrary new value \(T = t\)
This change propagates along directed paths out of \(T\) to all descendant variables of \(T\) in the graph, which can change their values

title: Machine learning
text:
Writing an intervention down
Behind a DAG is a structural model: one equation per variable, from its parents and its own noise. With \(T\) the target, \(Y\) the outcome and \(Z\) the other variables that matter: \[
T = h(Z, \varepsilon_T), \qquad Y = g(T, Z, \varepsilon_Y), \qquad Z,\ \varepsilon_T,\ \varepsilon_Y \text{ independent}
\]
Intervene on \(T\), written \(do(T = t)\): delete \(T\)’s equation and set \(T = t\). Every other equation stays, and the noises keep their distribution. \(Z\) keeps its distribution

title: Machine learning
section: Recovering the effect from what we observe
text:
Recovering the effect from what we observe
Under \(do(T = t)\), \(Y = g(t, Z, \varepsilon_Y)\) with \((Z, \varepsilon_Y)\) distributed as before, so \(\mathbb E[Y \mid do(T = t)] = \mathbb E\, g(t, Z, \varepsilon_Y)\). Compare \(\mathbb E[Y \mid T = t]\), the average over the units that happened to have \(T = t\)










From observed \((T, Z, Y)\): write down what you would compute to get \(\mathbb E[Y \mid do(T = t)]\), and what has to be true of \(Z\) for it to work.

title: Machine learning
text:
The confounding gap
The same DAG, made linear: \(T = \alpha Z + \varepsilon_T\), \(\;Y = \tau T + \beta Z + \varepsilon_Y\), with \(Z\), \(\varepsilon_T\), \(\varepsilon_Y\) independent normal and the noises mean \(0\) \[
\mathbb E[Y \mid do(T = 1)] - \mathbb E[Y \mid do(T = 0)] = \tau
\] \[
\mathbb E[Y \mid T = 1] - \mathbb E[Y \mid T = 0] = \tau + \beta\,\big(\mathbb E[Z \mid T = 1] - \mathbb E[Z \mid T = 0]\big)
\]

Week 2, omitted-variable bias, inputs fixed: regressing on \(\mathbf x_1\) alone gives \(\mathbb E\hat\beta_{\text{short}} = \beta_1 + \beta_2\hat\delta\), with \(\hat\delta\) the slope of \(\mathbf x_2\) on \(\mathbf x_1\).


The naive difference is the effect plus what \(Z\) contributes through selection: omitted-variable bias, read causally. Derivation: exercise 2.

title: Machine learning
text:
Adjustment theorem


Adjustment theorem. Structural model with independent noises, \(Z\) observed, \(T\) taking finitely many values: \(T = h(Z, \varepsilon_T)\), \(Y = g(T, Z, \varepsilon_Y)\). If \(P(T = t \mid Z) > 0\) with probability one, \[
\mathbb E[Y \mid do(T = t)] = \mathbb E_Z\Big[\, \mathbb E[Y \mid T = t, Z]\, \Big]
\]











Corollary (\(Z\) empty, \(T\) randomized): \(\mathbb E[Y \mid do(T = t)] = \mathbb E[Y \mid T = t]\).

Fix \(T\) at \(t\), average the conditional mean over the population’s \(Z\). In this model the condition, in words: \(Z\) holds every common cause of \(T\) and \(Y\) and no consequence of \(T\).

Proof: exercise 3 in the notebook, before the seminar.

title: Machine learning
text:
The propensity score
From here on \(T \in \{0, 1\}\): treated or not. The propensity score is the class probability from the first half of the lecture, with \(T\) as the label and \(Z\) as the input: \[
\pi(z) = P(T = 1 \mid Z = z)
\]
Logistic regression of \(T\) on \(Z\) estimates it: glm(T ~ Z, family = binomial())

Suppose you can estimate \(\pi(z)\) well, but you have no regression model for \(\mathbb E[Y \mid T, Z]\). How would you use \(\hat\pi\) to estimate \(\mathbb E[Y \mid do(T = 1)]\)?


Hint: make the data look as if \(T\) had been assigned by a coin flip, not by the confounders

title: Machine learning
text:
Inverse propensity weighting theorem
Inverse propensity weighting (IPW) theorem. Structural model with independent noises, \(Z\) observed, \(T \in \{0, 1\}\): \(T = h(Z, \varepsilon_T)\), \(Y = g(T, Z, \varepsilon_Y)\), \(\pi(z) = P(T = 1 \mid Z = z)\). If \(0 < \pi(Z) < 1\) with probability one, \[
\mathbb E[Y \mid do(T = 1)] = \mathbb E\Big[\frac{T\,Y}{\pi(Z)}\Big], \qquad \mathbb E[Y \mid do(T = 0)] = \mathbb E\Big[\frac{(1 - T)\,Y}{1 - \pi(Z)}\Big]
\]

Weight each treated unit by \(1/\pi(Z)\): it stands in for \(1/\pi(Z)\) units with the same \(Z\). The adjustment theorem needs a regression model for \(Y\). This one needs a regression model for \(T\), and logistic regression gives one.

Where inverse propensity weighting fails

\(\pi(Z)\) near \(0\) or \(1\): a few units get huge weights, and the estimate is unstable. The condition \(0 < \pi(Z) < 1\) is about the population; in a sample it shows up as extreme weights
Causal machine learning replaces logistic regression with more flexible models. If these models achieve high accuracy, they can output probabilities close to \(0\) or \(1\), and the weights explode: a better classifier can make a worse weighting estimate
A common cause left out of \(Z\): \(\varepsilon_T\) and \(\varepsilon_Y\) are dependent, and step (c) of the proof breaks

At a minimum of

Three errors, three names
Population risk of a predictor \(f\), an expectation over new data, the thing we want small: \[R(f) = \mathbb E\,\ell(Y, f(X))\]
Training error (empirical risk), the same average over the data we fit on: \[\hat R_n(f) = \tfrac{1}{n}\textstyle\sum_{i=1}^n \ell(y_i, f(x_i))\]
Test error, last week’s leaderboard, over held-out data: \[\widehat{\text{Err}} = \tfrac{1}{m}\textstyle\sum_{j=1}^m \ell(y_j^{\text{test}}, \hat f(x_j^{\text{test}}))\]

Optimal model theorem
Squared loss, any function of \(X\) allowed, not only lines:
\(\mathbb E Y^2 < \infty\) and \(f^\star(x) = \mathbb E[Y \mid X = x]\). For every \(f\) with \(\mathbb E f(X)^2 < \infty\), \[
R(f) = R(f^\star) + \mathbb E\big[(f^\star(X) - f(X))^2\big]
\]

Squared loss: the target is the conditional mean. Week 1’s \(f^\star\) is \(\mathbb E[Y \mid X]\), and the excess risk of any \(f\), any method, is one number.

Proof: exercise 1 in the notebook, before the seminar. Corollaries: absolute loss, the conditional median (stated, not proved); zero–one loss, next week.

\[

Notational conventions
We’ll use common conventions in this course

Bold for vectors, bold and upper case for matrices
Otherwise upper case denotes random variable
Error terms \(\varepsilon = y - \mathbf x^T \beta\) never truly observed
Residuals \(r = y - \mathbf x^T \hat \beta\) used as a proxy for errors
Greek letters like \(\beta, \theta, \sigma, \Sigma\) usually unknown parameters
Greek letters with hats like \(\hat \beta\) are estimates computed from data
Roman letters that usually denote functions with hats, like \(\hat f\) are also estimates

Least-squares solutions in matrix notation
With matrix-vector notation we can always write very simply:
\[
\hat {\mathbf \beta} = (\mathbf X^T\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf X^T \mathbf y = \mathbf X^\dagger \mathbf y
\]
Remember this! It encodes many important facts…

This assumes \(\mathbf X^T\mathbf X\) to be invertible, i.e. the columns of \(\mathbf X\) have full rank (columns = variables)

That’s often true if \(n > p\), unless some problem like one variable is a copy of another




Impossible if \(p \ge n\) (more columns than rows, the intercept counted). “High-dimensional” regression requires special methods, covered soon in this course!

Predictions from the linear model:
\[\hat{\mathbf y} = \mathbf {X} \hat{\mathbf \beta} = \mathbf X (\mathbf X^T\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf X^T \mathbf y = \mathbf H \mathbf y\] if we define
\[\mathbf H = \mathbf X (\mathbf X^T\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf X^T = \mathbf X \mathbf X^\dagger\]
(the pseudoinverse \(\mathbf X^\dagger\) of the previous slide: \(\hat{\mathbf y} = \mathbf X \hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = \mathbf X \mathbf X^\dagger \mathbf y\))

section: Linear algebra and geometric intuition, continued
text:
Linear algebra and geometric intuition, continued
COOL FACTS about \(\mathbf H\):

\(\mathbf H\) is a projection: \(\mathbf H^2 = \mathbf H\)
For any \(n\)-vector \(\mathbf v\), the \(n\)-vector \(\mathbf {Hv}\) is the orthogonal projection of \(\mathbf v\) onto the column space of \(\mathbf X\)
Of all linear combinations of columns of \(\mathbf X\), \(\mathbf {Hv}\) is the one closest (in Euclidean distance) to \(\mathbf v\).

title: Machine learning
text:
Partialling-out theorem (Frisch–Waugh–Lovell)
\(\mathbf X = [\mathbf X_1 \;\; \mathbf x_2]\), full column rank, the intercept column inside \(\mathbf X_1\). \(\mathbf M_1 = \mathbf I - \mathbf X_1(\mathbf X_1^T\mathbf X_1)^{-1}\mathbf X_1^T\) projects onto the orthogonal complement of \(\mathrm{col}(\mathbf X_1)\), so \(\tilde{\mathbf x}_2 = \mathbf M_1 \mathbf x_2\) is the residual of \(\mathbf x_2\) after regressing it on \(\mathbf X_1\). The coefficient on \(\mathbf x_2\) in the regression of \(\mathbf y\) on \(\mathbf X\) is \[
\hat\beta_2 = \frac{\tilde{\mathbf x}_2^T \mathbf y}{\tilde{\mathbf x}_2^T \tilde{\mathbf x}_2}
\] (and the same number comes from regressing \(\mathbf M_1 \mathbf y\) on \(\tilde{\mathbf x}_2\): residual on residual).

The coefficient on \(x_2\) is the slope of \(y\) on what is left of \(x_2\) after \(\mathbf X_1\) has explained what it can. Fitting to residuals: additive models, boosting and causal ML share the mechanism, not a guarantee.

title: Machine learning
text:
Visualizing orthogonal subspaces









Project everything onto the orthogonal complement of \(\mathrm{col}(\mathbf X_1)\), the grey plane. There, regress \(\tilde{\mathbf y}\) on \(\tilde{\mathbf x}_2\) through the origin: the slope is \(\hat\beta_2\) and \(\mathbf r\) is the full regression’s residual

title: Machine learning
text:
Partialling-out theorem, lines 1–2
The full regression, with the normal equations read column by column: the residual is orthogonal to every column \[
\mathbf y = \mathbf X_1 \hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_1 + \mathbf x_2 \hat\beta_2 + \mathbf r, \qquad \mathbf X_1^T \mathbf r = \mathbf 0,\ \ \mathbf x_2^T \mathbf r = 0
\]

Multiply through by \(\mathbf M_1\): \[
\mathbf M_1 \mathbf y = \mathbf M_1 \mathbf X_1 \hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_1 + \mathbf M_1 \mathbf x_2 \hat\beta_2 + \mathbf M_1 \mathbf r
\]


\(\mathbf M_1 \mathbf X_1 = \mathbf 0\) and \(\mathbf M_1 \mathbf r = \mathbf r\) (because \(\mathbf r \perp \mathrm{col}(\mathbf X_1)\)), so \[
\mathbf M_1 \mathbf y = \tilde{\mathbf x}_2 \,\hat\beta_2 + \mathbf r
\]

title: Machine learning
text:
Partialling-out theorem, lines 3–4
\(\mathbf M_1 \mathbf y = \tilde{\mathbf x}_2 \,\hat\beta_2 + \mathbf r\) is a vector equation with one unknown number, \(\hat\beta_2\)

Multiply by \(\tilde{\mathbf x}_2^T = \mathbf x_2^T \mathbf M_1\): \[
\tilde{\mathbf x}_2^T \mathbf M_1 \mathbf y = \tilde{\mathbf x}_2^T \tilde{\mathbf x}_2\, \hat\beta_2 + \tilde{\mathbf x}_2^T \mathbf r
\]


The last term: \(\tilde{\mathbf x}_2^T \mathbf r = \mathbf x_2^T \mathbf M_1 \mathbf r = \mathbf x_2^T \mathbf r = 0\)

title: Machine learning
text:
Partialling-out theorem, lines 5–6
Left side: \(\tilde{\mathbf x}_2^T \mathbf M_1 \mathbf y = \mathbf x_2^T \mathbf M_1 \mathbf M_1 \mathbf y\)

\(= \mathbf x_2^T \mathbf M_1 \mathbf y = \tilde{\mathbf x}_2^T \mathbf y\), using \(\mathbf M_1^T = \mathbf M_1 = \mathbf M_1^2\)


Full column rank makes \(\tilde{\mathbf x}_2^T \tilde{\mathbf x}_2 > 0\), so \[
\hat\beta_2 = \frac{\tilde{\mathbf x}_2^T \mathbf y}{\tilde{\mathbf x}_2^T \tilde{\mathbf x}_2} = \frac{\tilde{\mathbf x}_2^T \tilde{\mathbf y}}{\tilde{\mathbf x}_2^T \tilde{\mathbf x}_2}, \qquad \tilde{\mathbf y} = \mathbf M_1 \mathbf y \qquad \blacksquare
\]
(ESL §3.2.3.)

Prediction, loss, held-out set
Training data: \(n\) units \((x_i, y_i)\), \(i = 1, \ldots, n\), inputs \(x_i\) and outcomes \(y_i\), both known
Test data (held out): \(m\) more units \((x_j^{\text{test}}, y_j^{\text{test}})\), \(j = 1, \ldots, m\); competitors see only the \(x_j^{\text{test}}\)
A predictor \(\hat f\) is built from the training data alone
A loss scores one prediction: today, \(\ell(y, \hat y) = (y - \hat y)^2\)
The test error is the average loss over the test data: \[
\widehat{\text{Err}} = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{j=1}^{m} \ell\big(y_j^{\text{test}}, \hat f(x_j^{\text{test}})\big)
\]
That number is the leaderboard.

What makes a nearest-neighbor prediction wrong?
\(y_i = f^\star(x_i) + \varepsilon_i\), inputs fixed, noise independent, mean \(0\), variance \(\sigma^2\); new \(Y_0 = f^\star(x_0) + \varepsilon_0\).
We want \(\mathbb E\big[(Y_0 - \hat f_k(x_0))^2\big]\), the expected squared error of the \(k\)-nearest-neighbor prediction at \(x_0\).

Two facts from ST102 do all the work in the proof. Which two? Write them down before we start.

Bias–variance decomposition, line 1
\[
Y_0 - \hat f_k(x_0) = \varepsilon_0 + \big[f^\star(x_0) - \hat f_k(x_0)\big]
\]
Square, take expectations: \[
\mathbb E\big[(Y_0 - \hat f_k(x_0))^2\big] = \mathbb E[\varepsilon_0^2] + 2\,\mathbb E\big[\varepsilon_0 \,(f^\star(x_0) - \hat f_k(x_0))\big] + \mathbb E\big[(f^\star(x_0) - \hat f_k(x_0))^2\big]
\]

title: Machine learning
text:
Bias–variance decomposition, line 2
\(\varepsilon_0\) is independent of everything in \(\hat f_k(x_0)\) and has mean \(0\): \[
\mathbb E\big[\varepsilon_0 \,(f^\star(x_0) - \hat f_k(x_0))\big] = \mathbb E[\varepsilon_0]\; \mathbb E\big[f^\star(x_0) - \hat f_k(x_0)\big] = 0
\]
Left with \[
\sigma^2 + \mathbb E\big[(f^\star(x_0) - \hat f_k(x_0))^2\big]
\]

title: Machine learning
text:
Bias–variance decomposition, line 3
Add and subtract \(\mathbb E \hat f_k(x_0)\) inside the square: \[
\mathbb E\big[(f^\star(x_0) - \hat f_k(x_0))^2\big] = \big[f^\star(x_0) - \mathbb E\hat f_k(x_0)\big]^2 + \mathrm{Var}\big(\hat f_k(x_0)\big)
\]
(The cross term is \(2[f^\star(x_0) - \mathbb E\hat f_k(x_0)]\,\mathbb E[\mathbb E\hat f_k(x_0) - \hat f_k(x_0)] = 0\).)

title: Machine learning
text:
Bias–variance decomposition, lines 4 and 5
The neighborhood is fixed, so \[
\mathbb E\hat f_k(x_0) = \frac{1}{k}\sum_{l=1}^k f^\star(x_{(l)}),
\qquad
\mathrm{Var}\big(\hat f_k(x_0)\big) = \frac{1}{k^2}\sum_{l=1}^k \sigma^2 = \frac{\sigma^2}{k}
\]
Substitute: \[
\mathbb E\big[(Y_0 - \hat f_k(x_0))^2\big] = \sigma^2 + \Big[f^\star(x_0) - \tfrac{1}{k}\textstyle\sum_{l=1}^k f^\star(x_{(l)})\Big]^2 + \frac{\sigma^2}{k} \qquad \blacksquare
\]
(ESL §7.3, equation 7.10.)

title: Machine learning
text:
Distances concentrate

Why: \(\|X - X'\|^2/2d\) is an average of \(d\) independent coordinate terms, each with mean \(1\), so its spread falls like \(1/\sqrt d\): the same averaging that gave the bias–variance decomposition its variance term.

title: Machine learning
text:
Distance concentration
Distance concentration (stated, not proved). For \(X, X'\) independent \(N(0, I_d)\), \(\|X - X'\|^2/2d\) has mean \(1\) and variance \(2/d\), so by Chebyshev \[
\Pr\!\left( \Big| \tfrac{\|X - X'\|^2}{2d} - 1 \Big| > \varepsilon \right) \le \tfrac{2}{d\varepsilon^2},
\] and by a union bound over the \(n-1\) distances from a query point, every neighbor’s squared distance lies within \(2d(1 \pm \varepsilon)\) with probability at least \(1 - 2(n-1)/(d\varepsilon^2)\). So for \(n\) fixed as \(d\) grows, the nearest neighbor is about as far as the farthest.

title: About this course

References
These are all available free online at the links below.

ISLR: An Introduction to Statistical Learning with Applications in R
Our main text for most of the term. Readings are given by chapter and page from the second edition.


PPA: Patterns, Predictions, and Actions
Where the idea of machine learning as a prediction competition comes from, and our reference for a few topics that computer scientists cover and statisticians’ textbooks don’t.


CausalML: Applied Causal Inference Powered by ML and AI
A reference for the causal thread of the course (weeks 3, 8 and 10); assigned as optional deeper reading, and the natural next stop after week 10.


R4DS: R for Data Science
There are many good sources about R that you can find online, but this one has the advantage of offering one coherent point of view.


Going deeper
ESL (Elements of Statistical Learning) is the more advanced version of ISLR, by some of the same authors; most of the theorems in this course are in it somewhere. CASI (Computer Age Statistical Inference) has a different emphasis and some history. IML (Interpretable Machine Learning) is our reference for partial dependence, feature importance and Shapley values; we refer to it by chapter title because its chapter numbers keep changing.


Ethical guidelines
Brief documents published by professional societies on the ethical practice of statistics or data science. They are all worth reading and comparing: Royal Statistical Society, American Statistical Association, Association for Computing Machinery.

title: ST310 course page
section: Week 1: prediction competitions and nearest neighbors
text:
Week 1: prediction competitions and nearest neighbors
What machine learning is and where it came from: two lineages, one field, and the prediction competition (the common task framework) as its working definition, with the Netflix prize as the cautionary tale. A first prediction task, the rule that a prediction may use only what is available at prediction time, a held-out set as the score, and \(k\)-nearest neighbors as the first method. The bias–variance decomposition derived for \(k\)-NN at the board, and why nearest neighbors stop working in many dimensions.
Reading

ISLR Chapter 1 (Introduction), pp. 1–14. A quick read; don’t skip the section on notation and simple matrix algebra.
ISLR Chapter 2 (Statistical Learning), sections 2.1 and 2.2, pp. 15–42. If R is new to you, also do the lab in section 2.3, pp. 42–52.
PPA Chapter 1 (Introduction), pp. 1–10.

If you finish these quickly you may want to start Chapter 3, because it’s a long one.
Lecture: slides
Seminar: notebook (.qmd) · notebook with solutions

title: ST310 course page
text:
Week 2: linear regression
Regression as the first fitted model rather than a review: least squares and the hat matrix, and the conditional mean as the target that every regression method is aiming at (the optimal model theorem). Multiple regression and what a coefficient holds fixed: the partialling-out theorem, proved in the lecture and reused in weeks 8 and 10, and omitted-variable bias, what the same algebra says when a relevant column is left out.
Reading

ISLR Chapter 3 (Linear Regression), sections 3.1–3.3 and 3.5, pp. 61–110. Mostly review from your regression course; read 3.2.1 (estimating the coefficients in multiple regression) and 3.3.3 (potential problems) slowly. The lab in 3.6 goes with the seminar.
PPA Chapter 2 (Fundamentals of prediction), the sections “Modeling knowledge” and “Prediction via optimization”, pp. 13–21.

Optional, deeper: ESL section 2.4 (the optimal model theorem) and section 3.2, pp. 44–57 (3.2.3 is the partialling-out theorem).
Lecture: slides
Seminar: notebook (.qmd) · notebook with solutions. Before the seminar, do exercises 1 to 3 at the top of the notebook (the two proofs the lecture left to you, and the partialling-out proof again with the slides closed); the seminar’s problems start from them. Bring a dataset of your own if you have one: a numeric outcome and a few predictors, one row per unit.

title: ST310 course page
text:
Week 3: classification, and causality (part 1)
Classification: logistic regression, a threshold and the two kinds of error on either side of it, and the metrics that follow; the optimal threshold theorem says where the threshold goes, and the costs choose it. Causal block 1: prediction against intervention, a world in which the causation runs the other way from the correlation, and why a model that predicts well can still give the wrong answer to a what-if question. The adjustment theorem says when averaging over a measured variable recovers the effect of an intervention, and the inverse propensity weighting theorem, proved in the lecture, gets the same effect by weighting with the probability of treatment, a class probability that logistic regression estimates.
Reading

ISLR Chapter 4 (Classification), sections 4.1–4.3, pp. 130–141. Section 4.4 (LDA, QDA, naive Bayes) is not part of this course; skim 4.5, pp. 158–164, for the comparison with \(k\)-nearest neighbors.
PPA Chapter 9 (Causality), from “The limitations of observation” through “Confounding”, pp. 179–192.

Optional: PPA Chapter 2 (Fundamentals of prediction), “Types of errors and successes” and “The Neyman–Pearson lemma”, pp. 21–26, and “Decisions that discriminate”, pp. 26–31.
Lecture: slides
Seminar: notebook (.qmd) · notebook with solutions. Before the seminar, do exercises 1 to 4 at the top of the notebook (the threshold proof, the confounding gap, the adjustment proof, and the lecture’s inverse propensity weighting proof again with the slides closed); the seminar’s problems start from them. Data: the Palmer penguins (data note); the (fictional) attrition data as an alternative.

title: ST310 course page
text:
Week 4: optimization and model fitting
How a model actually gets fitted. Logistic regression first: maximum likelihood, the score equations read as week 2’s orthogonality, and why there is no closed form. Then the method that fits almost everything else: gradient descent, step sizes and the descent lemma, and its stochastic version, whose random steps are unbiased for the full gradient. Empirical risk minimization as the common form of every method so far, the bias–variance decomposition in that form, why no method is best on every problem, and early stopping as a first kind of regularization.
Reading

PPA Chapter 5 (Optimization), from “Optimization basics” through “The SGD quick start guide”, pp. 70–86, stopping at “Analysis of the stochastic gradient method”: gradient descent, the quadratic case, and stochastic gradient descent in practice.

Optional: PPA “Analysis of the stochastic gradient method”, pp. 86–88 (a convergence bound), and “Regularization” with “Implicit regularization by optimization”, pp. 92–94 (why gradient descent from zero lands on the minimum-norm solution, which the seminar meets); ESL section 4.4.1 for Newton-IRLS in full; the Wikipedia pages on Newton’s method and gradient descent for pictures and animations.
Lecture: slides
Seminar: notebook (.qmd). Before the seminar, do exercises 1 to 4 at the top of the notebook (the lecture’s descent lemma again with the slides closed, the ERM form of the bias–variance decomposition, the logistic Hessian and the Newton-Raphson update, and no free lunch on a finite domain); the seminar’s problems start from them. You write gradient descent once, as a function, and use it for least squares, logistic regression and random batches. Data: gapminder and the Palmer penguins (data note), then simulated data.

title: ST310 course page
text:
Week 5: functional structures
The methods, introduced together and compared on one task, each a different functional structure for the predictor. Ridge and lasso: what a penalty changes and what \(\lambda\) controls. Additive models: a spline as regression on basis functions, one curve per input, the basis size as the knob. Trees: how a small tree predicts and why it is unstable; a random forest as many trees combined into one model. A neural network as a composition, a GLM whose inputs are the outputs of other GLMs, named and fitted and otherwise left for later. Then one simulated dataset for each kind of truth (sparse linear, additive smooth, a step in two inputs at once), every family fitted to each, and the four dimensions on which a method bets: wide or tall, sparse or dense, smooth or discontinuous, additive or interactive. Training error flatters a fitted model (the optimism theorem, stated; its proof is yours before the seminar). The three-way split, training, selection and a test set opened once, is used from the first slide. Data: Spotify tracks, what makes a song popular.
Reading

ISLR Chapter 6 (Linear Model Selection and Regularization), sections 6.2.1–6.2.2, pp. 237–250: ridge regression and the lasso, and what each penalty does to the coefficients. Stop before 6.2.3; choosing \(\lambda\) by cross-validation is week 7.
ISLR Chapter 7 (Moving Beyond Linearity), sections 7.3–7.4, pp. 294–301 (basis functions and regression splines), and section 7.7, pp. 306–310 (generalized additive models; 7.7.1 fits one by least squares on spline basis functions, as the lecture does, and the GAM part of the lab in 7.8 has the lm and ns() code). Section 7.5, smoothing splines, is week 7. Skim 7.6, pp. 304–306: local regression, not examined.
ISLR Chapter 8 (Tree-Based Methods), section 8.1.1, pp. 328–335 (regression trees), and sections 8.2.1–8.2.2, pp. 340–345 (bagging and random forests). Skim 8.1.2–8.1.4, pp. 335–340. Section 8.2.3, boosting, is week 8.

Optional: PPA Chapter 6 (Generalization), “Generalization gap”, pp. 100–101, the setting of the optimism theorem.
Lecture and seminar: released here at the start of the week. Every family and the baselines on the Spotify tracks (data note), one leaderboard, the three-way split enforced.

title: ST310 course page
text:
Week 6: reading week
No lecture or seminar. Start week 7’s reading: ISLR section 5.1, pp. 197–209 (cross-validation), which week 7 opens with.

title: ST310 course page
section: Week 7: how much flexibility should we allow?
text:
Week 7: how much flexibility should we allow?
Every method of week 5 had a knob. This week chooses it, and asks what the choice costs. \(K\)-fold cross-validation and the curve it draws against \(\lambda\), \(k\) and tree depth. Why a flexible method needs data: from week 1’s decomposition, the error of \(k\)-nearest neighbors in \(d\) dimensions, the rate \(n^{-2/(d+2)}\), and what an assumption buys (an additive truth, a sparse one). Ridge and lasso side by side in the simplest design: shrinkage against soft thresholding, prediction against selection; the smoothing penalty on a spline as ridge on its coefficients. What changes when \(p > n\): the minimum-norm interpolant, why one interpolant rather than another, and the double-descent curve that the bias–variance picture does not predict. The standard error of a held-out score.
Reading [PROVISIONAL]

ISLR Chapter 5 (Resampling Methods), section 5.1, pp. 197–209 (the validation set, leave-one-out and \(K\)-fold cross-validation, and the bias–variance trade-off in choosing \(K\)). Section 5.2, the bootstrap, is not part of this course.
ISLR Chapter 6, section 6.2.3, pp. 250–252 (choosing the tuning parameter by cross-validation), and section 6.4, from p. 261 (what changes when \(p > n\)). Section 6.3, which sits between them, is not part of this course.
ISLR Chapter 7, section 7.5, pp. 301–304 (smoothing splines: the roughness penalty, and \(\lambda\) chosen from the data).
PPA Chapter 6 (Generalization), “Generalization gap” and “Overparameterization: empirical phenomena”, pp. 100–106 (what over-parameterized models do in practice; double descent).

Deeper, optional: Belkin, Hsu, Ma and Mandal, “Reconciling modern machine-learning practice and the classical bias–variance trade-off”, PNAS 116(32), 2019 (the double-descent curve); ESL section 3.4, pp. 61–73 (ridge and the lasso in general designs); Györfi, Kohler, Krzyżak and Walk, A Distribution-Free Theory of Nonparametric Regression (2002), Chapter 6, for the rigorous form of the nearest-neighbor rate the lecture derives from a stated lemma.
Lecture and seminar: released here at the start of the week. A cross-validation pipeline on week 5’s data; learning curves for \(k\)-nearest neighbors in one, two, five and ten dimensions read against the rate; then, after cross-validation has worked for you, two ways it goes wrong: standardizing before the split against inside the folds, and a random split against a split in time. Data: week 5’s datasets, ISLR’s Hitters (baseball salaries, 1987), simulated data.

title: ST310 course page
section: Week 8: how are flexible models constructed and improved?
text:
Week 8: how are flexible models constructed and improved?
How the fits of week 5 are built, and what makes them better. An additive model by backfitting: each component fitted to what the others leave, which is week 2’s partialling-out theorem one input at a time; and an interaction that no additive fit can see. A tree: one split found by hand, then greedy recursion, depth and pruning, and why a tree is unstable. Bagging: the variance of an average of correlated predictions, proved, and why it stops short of \(1/B\); random forests as the way to lower the correlation; the out-of-bag error as a held-out score that comes free. Boosting as gradient descent one small tree at a time (week 4’s method on week 2’s residuals), its three knobs, and why a sum of trees is additive in trees and not in the predictors. Two slides on kernels: a locally weighted average with a bandwidth, and ridge on features you never write down.
Reading [PROVISIONAL]

ESL Chapter 9, the opening of section 9.1, pp. 295–298 (additive models and the backfitting algorithm, Algorithm 9.1). ISLR section 7.7, pp. 306–310, read in week 5, describes the same model.
ISLR Chapter 8 (Tree-Based Methods), section 8.1, pp. 327–340, in full this time (recursive binary splitting and pruning; classification trees; trees against linear models), and sections 8.2.1–8.2.3, pp. 340–348 (bagging, random forests, boosting). Section 8.2.4, Bayesian additive regression trees, is not part of this course. The lab in section 8.3 goes with the seminar.
ESL Chapter 15, section 15.4, pp. 597–602 (why random forests work: the variance of a correlated average, which is the lecture’s proof).

Deeper, optional: ESL sections 10.9–10.10, pp. 353–361 (boosting trees as gradient descent); ESL Chapter 6, section 6.1 (one-dimensional kernel smoothers), for the kernel slides; Breiman, “Random forests”, Machine Learning 45, 2001; Friedman, “Greedy function approximation: a gradient boosting machine”, Annals of Statistics 29(5), 2001.
Lecture and seminar: released here at the start of the week. One split by hand, then a recursive tree; backfitting in ten lines against mgcv; bagging by hand with its variance measured against the theorem and an out-of-bag error; one boosting update by hand, then xgboost. Data: the penguins, the movies, gapminder, simulated data.

title: ST310 course page
section: Week 9: what can we learn from a fitted prediction?
text:
Week 9: what can we learn from a fitted prediction?
What a forecast is for. The decision principle: choose the action that minimizes expected loss given the inputs. The mean, the median and week 3’s threshold were three cases of it; the conditional quantile is the fourth, and the lecture proves it. Uncertainty about a future outcome, which is not uncertainty about a score: a prediction interval from estimated quantiles, by linear quantile regression and then by a method of week 5, with a Gaussian mean-and-variance model as the comparison; coverage checked on fresh data across the range of the inputs, as a diagnostic and not a certificate; why no distribution-free method can guarantee coverage at every \(x\), and what conformal prediction guarantees instead; a calibration check for a classifier. Then interpretation of the models you can now fit: a coefficient under correlated inputs, a GAM’s components, permutation importance and where it fails, partial dependence and ICE as questions put to the model (SHAP named in one slide), and why a model’s response curve is not an effect.
Reading [PROVISIONAL]

Koenker and Hallock, “Quantile regression”, Journal of Economic Perspectives 15(4), 2001, pp. 143–156: the first half, for what a conditional quantile is and the loss that finds it.
ISLR Chapter 3, section 3.2.2, the passage on confidence and prediction intervals (p. 82): the distinction the lecture starts from.
IML, the chapters “Partial dependence plot (PDP)”, “Individual conditional expectation (ICE)” and “Permutation feature importance”: the definitions and the pictures. The chapter “SHAP” is for recognition only.

Deeper, optional: Angelopoulos and Bates, “Conformal prediction: a gentle introduction”, Foundations and Trends in Machine Learning 16(4), 2023, sections 1–2; Barber, Candès, Ramdas and Tibshirani, “The limits of distribution-free conditional predictive inference”, Information and Inference 10(2), 2021 (the impossibility result the lecture states); Zhao and Hastie, “Causal interpretations of black-box models”, Journal of Business and Economic Statistics 39(1), 2021.
Lecture and seminar: released here at the start of the week. A simulation whose noise grows with one input: quantile fits, interval widths and coverage by range on fresh data; the calibration of week 3’s logistic fit; partial dependence, ICE and permutation importance by hand on week 8’s models. Data: supplied simulations, the penguins, the movies.

title: ST310 course page
section: Week 10: how do prediction methods support other statistical tasks?
text:
Week 10: how do prediction methods support other statistical tasks?
A fitted model put to a use other than predicting. A partial dependence curve as an estimate of week 3’s interventional mean, exact at the population level when the adjustment condition holds and the model is right, and an estimate otherwise. One effect estimated with machine learning doing the nuisance work: residual on residual, the two lines that show why residualizing the treatment makes the nuisance error second order (the lecture’s derivation), what cross-fitting does, a standard error that can be trusted, and honest trees as the same split-sample idea; nothing in any of it makes the effect causal without week 3’s condition. Then the data move: covariate shift and reweighting by a ratio of probabilities (week 3’s inverse propensity weighting again), label shift and which factorization of the joint distribution you believe, and adaptive drift when the model has been tuned to the score it is judged by.
Reading [PROVISIONAL]

PPA Chapter 10 (Causal inference in practice), pp. 204–217: design and inference, adjustment and controls, reductions to model fitting (double machine learning in a page), quasi-experiments, and the limitations.
PPA Chapter 8 (Datasets), “Longevity of benchmarks”, pp. 158–167 (what happens when the same held-out set is used many times, and the CIFAR-10 and ImageNet replications).
Zhao and Hastie, “Causal interpretations of black-box models”, Journal of Business and Economic Statistics 39(1), 2021 (the back-door statement behind the lecture’s corollary).

Deeper, optional: Chernozhukov, Chetverikov, Demirer, Duflo, Hansen, Newey and Robins, “Double/debiased machine learning for treatment and structural parameters”, Econometrics Journal 21(1), 2018, sections 1–2; Shimodaira, “Improving predictive inference under covariate shift by weighting the log-likelihood function”, Journal of Statistical Planning and Inference 90(2), 2000; Lipton, Wang and Smola, “Detecting and correcting for label shift with black box predictors”, ICML 2018 (the setting; the correction itself is not taught); PPA Chapter 13 (Epilogue), pp. 268–271.
Lecture and seminar: released here at the start of the week. One effect estimated by residual on residual with cross-fitting, two wrong versions and a hidden confounder; a partial dependence curve against the true interventional mean on a simulation; reweighting under covariate shift and under label shift, and a shift diagnosed on gapminder 1952 against 2007. Data: supplied simulations, gapminder.

title: ST310 course page
section: Week 11: what changes when the representation is learned?
text:
Week 11: what changes when the representation is learned?
Every method in this course was a predictor on features someone chose. What changes when the features are built by hand (week 8’s bases and kernels), learned together with the task (a network with one hidden layer as a basis the data chooses, fitted by week 4’s stochastic gradient descent; everything beyond that is ST311’s), or transferred from a model trained on something else (embeddings, with week 1’s nearest neighbors and week 5’s ridge run on them). Then the course’s frame read again with everything since: what the held-out leaderboard delivered, and where it stops, each limit being a result from the term. The theorems in one view, as a reference sheet.
Reading [PROVISIONAL]

PPA Chapter 4 (Representations and features), pp. 49–67: measurement, and “Nonlinear predictors” (polynomials, kernels and random features, and a neural network as a learned representation).
ISLR Chapter 10, sections 10.1–10.2, pp. 404–411 (single- and multilayer neural networks), for the one network the lecture builds. The rest of Chapter 10 is ST311’s.

Delivered in lecture, for reference rather than preparation:

Rodu and Baiocchi, “When black box algorithms are (not) appropriate”, Observational Studies 9(2), 2023 (arXiv 2001.07648): the common task framework and what it does and does not establish.
Wang, Kapoor, Barocas and Narayanan, “Against predictive optimization”, ACM Journal on Responsible Computing 1(1), 2024.

Optional: ISLR Chapter 12, section 12.2, from p. 498 (principal components, the simplest learned representation); Belkin, Hsu, Ma and Mandal, PNAS 2019, if not read in week 7.
Lecture and seminar: released here at the start of the week, together with the theorems in one view (statements only, with the week each was proved or derived; bring it to the seminar and try to reproduce each statement from memory first, checking second). Supplied text embeddings in R: \(k\)-nearest neighbors, ridge and logistic regression fitted on them, what the representation preserves and where evaluation fails; then one unfamiliar problem taken from target to evaluation. Data: a supplied embedding file, and your project data.

text:
Before the seminar

The lecture proved one result, which you redo with the slides closed (exercise 2), and stated another without proof, which you prove (exercise 3). Do all three exercises on paper before the seminar; the seminar’s problems are variations on exercise 2. You may use, without proof, two facts from ST102: for independent random variables the expectation of a product is the product of the expectations, and the variance of a sum is the sum of the variances.






WarningHints



Exercises 2 and 3 have hints, collapsed below them. Do not open a hint unless you have been stuck for at least a few minutes, and open them in order. Exercise 2’s proof is on the lecture slides. Solutions are shown in the seminar if you ask.


Exercise 1 (the competition). Without looking anything up: for the gapminder data, write down the four parts of a prediction competition (the unit, the inputs and outcome, the score, how the held-out set is chosen). Then, for each input: would you have it at the moment you need the prediction, for a country whose life expectancy you don’t know? “All of them” is an acceptable answer if you can say why.
Exercise 2 (bias–variance decomposition). The lecture proved this one. Close the slides and prove it again. The training data are \(y_i = f^\star(x_i) + \varepsilon_i\), \(i = 1, \ldots, n\), with the inputs fixed and the noise terms independent, each with mean \(0\) and variance \(\sigma^2\). A new outcome at the input \(x_0\) is \(Y_0 = f^\star(x_0) + \varepsilon_0\), where \(\varepsilon_0\) has the same mean and variance and is independent of the training noise. The prediction is \(\hat f_k(x_0) = \frac1k \sum_{l=1}^k y_{(l)}\), the average outcome of the \(k\) training points nearest to \(x_0\). Show that \[
\mathbb E\big[(Y_0 - \hat f_k(x_0))^2\big] = \sigma^2 + \Big[f^\star(x_0) - \tfrac{1}{k}\textstyle\sum_{l=1}^k f^\star(x_{(l)})\Big]^2 + \frac{\sigma^2}{k}.
\] Independence is used twice. Where?






NoteHint 1





Write \(Y_0 - \hat f_k(x_0) = \varepsilon_0 + \big[f^\star(x_0) - \hat f_k(x_0)\big]\). Square it and take expectations: three terms.









NoteHint 2





The middle term is \(2\,\mathbb E[\varepsilon_0\, g]\) with \(g = f^\star(x_0) - \hat f_k(x_0)\), a function of the training data. What does independence let you do to the expectation of a product?









NoteHint 3





You are left with \(\sigma^2 + \mathbb E[Z^2]\) for \(Z = f^\star(x_0) - \hat f_k(x_0)\). For any random variable, \(\mathbb E[Z^2] = (\mathbb E Z)^2 + \mathrm{Var}(Z)\).









NoteHint 4





Write \(\hat f_k(x_0)\) out in terms of \(f^\star\) and the noise. Which parts of it are random? Then take its mean and its variance.



Exercise 3 (distance concentration). The lecture stated this one without proof. Let \(X\) and \(X'\) be independent \(N(0, I_d)\) vectors and let \(W = \|X - X'\|^2/2d\). You may use that a standard normal \(Z\) has \(\mathbb E Z^4 = 3\).

Show that \(\mathbb E W = 1\) and \(\mathrm{Var}(W) = 2/d\).
Deduce that \(\Pr(|W - 1| > \varepsilon) \le 2/(d\varepsilon^2)\) for every \(\varepsilon > 0\).
Now take a query point and \(n - 1\) other points, all independent \(N(0, I_d)\). Show that with probability at least \(1 - 2(n-1)/(d\varepsilon^2)\), every one of the \(n - 1\) squared distances from the query lies between \(2d(1 - \varepsilon)\) and \(2d(1 + \varepsilon)\). The \(n - 1\) distances are not independent of each other. Why not, and why does your argument not need them to be?







NoteHint 1





Coordinate \(j\) of \(X - X'\) is a difference of two independent standard normals. What is its distribution? Write it as a multiple of a standard normal \(Z_j\).









NoteHint 2





Then \(W = \frac1d \sum_{j=1}^d Z_j^2\), an average of \(d\) independent terms. Find the mean and the variance of one term; problem 2(a) does the rest.









NoteHint 3





Part (b) is Chebyshev’s inequality: \(\Pr(|W - \mathbb E W| > \varepsilon) \le \mathrm{Var}(W)/\varepsilon^2\).









NoteHint 4





For (c): “some distance falls outside the range” is a union of \(n - 1\) events. How large can the probability of a union be?

Problems

These four problems rebuild the pieces of the lecture’s bias–variance decomposition. They use nothing beyond first-year probability.
Problem 1. Let \(Z\) be a random variable with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\).

Show that \(\mathbb E[Z^2] = \sigma^2 + \mu^2\).
In the lecture’s model \(Y_0 = f^\star(x_0) + \varepsilon_0\), the noise has mean \(0\) and variance \(\sigma^2\). What is \(\mathbb E[\varepsilon_0^2]\)?
Now let \(Z = f^\star(x_0) - \hat f(x_0)\), where \(f^\star(x_0)\) is a fixed number and \(\hat f(x_0)\) is a random predictor with mean \(m\) and variance \(v\). Write \(\mathbb E[Z^2]\) in terms of \(f^\star(x_0)\), \(m\) and \(v\). Which piece is a bias, and which a variance?

Problem 2. Let \(Y_1, \ldots, Y_k\) be independent random variables, each with variance \(\sigma^2\), and let \(\bar Y = \frac1k \sum_{l=1}^k Y_l\).

What is \(\mathrm{Var}(\bar Y)\)? Say where independence is used.
Suppose instead that \(Y_1 = Y_2 = \cdots = Y_k\) (the same random variable repeated). What is \(\mathrm{Var}(\bar Y)\) now? What does this say about averaging things that are not really different?

Problem 3. In the lecture’s setting, the new outcome’s noise \(\varepsilon_0\) has mean \(0\) and is independent of the training data. Let \(g\) be any function of the training data (for example, \(g = f^\star(x_0) - \hat f_k(x_0)\)).

Show that \(\mathbb E[\varepsilon_0\, g] = 0\).
Give an example where \(\mathbb E[\varepsilon_0] = 0\) but \(\mathbb E[\varepsilon_0\, g] \neq 0\). (Think about what happens if the “new” point is one of the training points.)
