title: Week 2 seminar
text:
Before the seminar

The lecture stated two results and left their proofs to you (exercises 1 and 2), and proved a third, which you redo with the slides closed (exercise 3). Do all three on paper before the seminar; the seminar’s problems are variations on the first two. You may use, without proof, two facts about conditional expectation from ST102: the tower property, \(\mathbb E[Z] = \mathbb E\big[\mathbb E[Z \mid X]\big]\), and taking out what is known, \(\mathbb E[g(X)\, Z \mid X] = g(X)\, \mathbb E[Z \mid X]\) for any function \(g\) of \(X\) (given \(X\), a function of \(X\) is a constant).






WarningHints



Each exercise has hints, collapsed below it. Do not open a hint unless you have been stuck for at least a few minutes, and open them in order. Exercise 3’s proof is on the lecture slides. Solutions to exercises 1 and 2 are shown in the seminar if you ask.


Exercise 1 (optimal model theorem). Let \(\mathbb E Y^2 < \infty\), \(f^\star(x) = \mathbb E[Y \mid X = x]\) and \(R(f) = \mathbb E\big[(Y - f(X))^2\big]\). Show that for every \(f\) with \(\mathbb E f(X)^2 < \infty\), \[
R(f) = R(f^\star) + \mathbb E\big[(f^\star(X) - f(X))^2\big].
\] Conclude that \(f^\star\) has the smallest risk of all functions of \(X\), and that the excess risk of any \(f\), fitted by any method, is the one number \(\mathbb E[(f^\star(X) - f(X))^2]\).






NoteHint 1





Add and subtract \(f^\star(X)\) inside the square, then expand.









NoteHint 2





Show that the cross term, \(\mathbb E\big[(Y - f^\star(X))\,(f^\star(X) - f(X))\big]\), is zero.









NoteHint 3





Condition on \(X\) first (the tower property), then take out what is known.



Exercise 2 (omitted-variable bias). Two predictors matter: \(\mathbf y = \beta_1 \mathbf x_1 + \beta_2 \mathbf x_2 + \boldsymbol\varepsilon\), all vectors in \(\mathbb R^n\) and centered (the intercept partialled out, as in the lecture). What is fixed: the inputs \(\mathbf x_1\) and \(\mathbf x_2\), which we condition on. What is random: the noise, with \(\mathbb E\,\boldsymbol\varepsilon = \mathbf 0\), and through it \(\mathbf y\). Somebody regresses \(\mathbf y\) on \(\mathbf x_1\) alone and reports \(\hat\beta_{\text{short}} = \mathbf x_1^T\mathbf y / \mathbf x_1^T\mathbf x_1\), random through \(\mathbf y\). Show that \[
\mathbb E\big[\hat\beta_{\text{short}} \mid \mathbf x_1, \mathbf x_2\big] = \beta_1 + \beta_2\,\hat\delta, \qquad \hat\delta = \frac{\mathbf x_1^T\mathbf x_2}{\mathbf x_1^T\mathbf x_1},
\] say in words what \(\hat\delta\) is, and say why it carries no randomness. When is the short regression unbiased for \(\beta_1\)?






NoteHint 1





Substitute the model for \(\mathbf y\) inside \(\mathbf x_1^T\mathbf y\) and split the fraction into three terms.









NoteHint 2





Two of the three terms are numbers once the inputs are fixed. Only the noise term is random: what is its expectation given the inputs?



Exercise 3 (partialling-out theorem). The lecture proved this one. Close the slides and prove it again. \(\mathbf X = [\mathbf X_1 \;\; \mathbf x_2]\) has full column rank, with the intercept column inside \(\mathbf X_1\); \(\mathbf M_1 = \mathbf I - \mathbf X_1(\mathbf X_1^T\mathbf X_1)^{-1}\mathbf X_1^T\) and \(\tilde{\mathbf x}_2 = \mathbf M_1\mathbf x_2\). You may use that \(\mathbf M_1\) is symmetric, that \(\mathbf M_1^2 = \mathbf M_1\) and that \(\mathbf M_1\mathbf X_1 = \mathbf 0\) (optional problem 4 proves all three). Show that the coefficient on \(\mathbf x_2\) in the least-squares regression of \(\mathbf y\) on \(\mathbf X\) is \[
\hat\beta_2 = \frac{\tilde{\mathbf x}_2^T \mathbf y}{\tilde{\mathbf x}_2^T \tilde{\mathbf x}_2},
\] and that regressing \(\tilde{\mathbf y} = \mathbf M_1\mathbf y\) on \(\tilde{\mathbf x}_2\) gives the same number. Where is full column rank used?






NoteHint 1





Start from the full regression and its normal equations: \(\mathbf y = \mathbf X_1\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_1 + \mathbf x_2\hat\beta_2 + \mathbf r\), with \(\mathbf X_1^T\mathbf r = \mathbf 0\) and \(\mathbf x_2^T\mathbf r = 0\). Which matrix removes the \(\mathbf X_1\) term?









NoteHint 2





Multiply through by \(\mathbf M_1\) and say what happens to each of the three terms on the right. For the last one, write \(\mathbf M_1\mathbf r = \mathbf r - \mathbf X_1(\mathbf X_1^T\mathbf X_1)^{-1}\mathbf X_1^T\mathbf r\).









NoteHint 3





You now have \(\mathbf M_1\mathbf y = \tilde{\mathbf x}_2\,\hat\beta_2 + \mathbf r\): a vector equation with one unknown number. Multiply by a row vector that turns it into a scalar equation in which the coefficient of \(\hat\beta_2\) is positive.









NoteHint 4





After multiplying by \(\tilde{\mathbf x}_2^T = \mathbf x_2^T\mathbf M_1\), two things remain: the term \(\tilde{\mathbf x}_2^T\mathbf r\), and an extra \(\mathbf M_1\) on the left side. Each goes away by one of the properties of \(\mathbf M_1\) you were given.

title: Week 2 seminar
text:
Problems

Problem 1 (the constant predictor). The setting of exercise 1.

Take \(f\) to be a constant \(c\). Which \(c\) minimizes \(R(c)\), and what is \(R(c)\) at the minimum? Express the answer in terms of \(R(f^\star)\) and \(\mathrm{Var}\big(f^\star(X)\big)\).
Deduce that \(\mathrm{Var}(Y) = R(f^\star) + \mathrm{Var}\big(f^\star(X)\big)\), and write both terms on the right as conditional moments of \(Y\) given \(X\). Which identity from ST102 is this?
Week 1 scored methods by squared error on held-out data. Imagine two oracle entries: one predicts \(\mathbb E Y\) for everyone, the other is \(f^\star\). What is the gap between their risks? On an actual leaderboard the constant entry uses the training mean \(\bar y\) and the best entry is some fitted \(\hat f\); give two reasons the observed gap need not equal that quantity. For a predictor fitted and chosen without using the test set, can its expected held-out squared error be below \(R(f^\star)\)?

Problem 2 (leaving a variable out, exactly). The setting of exercise 2, but forget the truth: let \(\hat\beta_1\) and \(\hat\beta_2\) be the least-squares coefficients from the long regression of \(\mathbf y\) on both \(\mathbf x_1\) and \(\mathbf x_2\), with residual \(\mathbf r\), so that \(\mathbf y = \hat\beta_1\mathbf x_1 + \hat\beta_2\mathbf x_2 + \mathbf r\).

Show that \(\hat\beta_{\text{short}} = \hat\beta_1 + \hat\beta_2\,\hat\delta\) exactly, with no expectation. Which fact about \(\mathbf r\) did you use?
Numbers: \(\mathbf x_1 = (-1, 0, 1)\), \(\mathbf x_2 = (-2, 1, 1)\), \(\beta_1 = 1\), \(\beta_2 = 2\). Compute \(\hat\delta\), and what the short regression estimates on average.
Suppose \(\mathbf x_1^T\mathbf x_2 = 0\). What happens to the coefficient on \(\mathbf x_1\) when \(\mathbf x_2\) is dropped? Reconcile your answer with the partialling-out theorem: what is the residual of \(\mathbf x_1\) after regressing it on \(\mathbf x_2\)?


Optional, can be done at home

Problem 3 (normal equations, and centering). Simple regression, from the lecture’s “nice geometry” slide. The training error is \(\hat R_n(\alpha, \beta) = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \alpha - \beta x_i)^2\).

Compute \(\partial \hat R_n/\partial\alpha\) and \(\partial \hat R_n/\partial\beta\), set both to zero, and show that the residuals \(r_i = y_i - \hat\alpha - \hat\beta x_i\) satisfy \(\sum_i r_i = 0\) and \(\sum_i x_i r_i = 0\). Write the same two equations as \(\mathbf X^T \mathbf r = \mathbf 0\) with \(\mathbf X = [\mathbf 1 \;\; \mathbf x]\).
Solve them: show \(\hat\beta = \sum_i (x_i - \bar x)(y_i - \bar y) \big/ \sum_i (x_i - \bar x)^2\) and \(\hat\alpha = \bar y - \hat\beta \bar x\).
In the partialling-out theorem take \(\mathbf X_1 = \mathbf 1\), the column of ones, and \(\mathbf x_2 = \mathbf x\). What is \(\mathbf M_1 \mathbf x\)? Conclude that the slope of \(\mathbf y\) on \(\mathbf x\) in a regression with an intercept is the slope through the origin of the centered \(\mathbf y\) on the centered \(\mathbf x\), and check that this is (b).







NoteHint 1






Differentiate one term of the sum first. (b) Use the first equation to eliminate \(\hat\alpha\) from the second.










NoteHint 2






\(\mathbf H_1 = \mathbf 1(\mathbf 1^T\mathbf 1)^{-1}\mathbf 1^T\): what is \(\mathbf 1^T\mathbf 1\), and what does \(\mathbf H_1\) do to a vector?




Problem 4 (the hat matrix). \(\mathbf X\) is \(n \times q\) with full column rank (\(q = p + 1\) columns, the intercept counted), \(\mathbf H = \mathbf X(\mathbf X^T\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf X^T\) and \(\mathbf M = \mathbf I - \mathbf H\).

Show \(\mathbf H^2 = \mathbf H\) and \(\mathbf H^T = \mathbf H\), and compute \(\mathrm{tr}(\mathbf H)\).
Show \(\mathbf M^2 = \mathbf M\), \(\mathbf M^T = \mathbf M\) and \(\mathbf M \mathbf X = \mathbf 0\). In one sentence each: what is \(\mathbf H\mathbf y\), and what is \(\mathbf M\mathbf y\)?
Use (b) to show that the residual vector \(\mathbf r = \mathbf M\mathbf y\) satisfies \(\mathbf X^T \mathbf r = \mathbf 0\) (the normal equations again, from the geometry instead of the calculus). Where did full column rank get used?







NoteHint 1






For the trace, \(\mathrm{tr}(\mathbf A\mathbf B) = \mathrm{tr}(\mathbf B\mathbf A)\) with \(\mathbf A = \mathbf X\).










NoteHint 2






Write \(\mathbf X^T\mathbf r = \mathbf X^T\mathbf M\mathbf y\) and use \(\mathbf M^T = \mathbf M\) to move \(\mathbf M\) onto \(\mathbf X\).




Problem 5 (a zero slope with a predictable outcome). Let \(X\) take the values \(-1, 0, 1\) with probability \(1/3\) each, let \(\varepsilon\) be independent of \(X\) and take the values \(-1, 1\) with probability \(1/2\) each, and let \(Y = X^2 + \varepsilon\).

Find \(f^\star(x)\) under squared loss, and its risk \(R(f^\star)\).
Find the best linear predictor \(a + bX\), the minimizer of \(\mathbb E[(Y - a - bX)^2]\), and its risk. Compute \(\mathrm{Cov}(X, Y)\).
What does the example say about using correlation to decide whether \(X\) predicts \(Y\)? Which result from the lecture gives the excess risk of the best line, and what is it here?







NoteHint 1






\(\mathbb E[Y \mid X = x]\) is \(x^2\) plus the mean of the noise.










NoteHint 2






The best line’s slope is \(\mathrm{Cov}(X, Y)/\mathrm{Var}(X)\); compute \(\mathbb E X^3\). Its risk is then the variance of something.




Problem 6 (why collinearity makes a coefficient uncertain). Fixed design: \(\mathbf y = \mathbf X_1\boldsymbol\beta_1 + \mathbf x_2\beta_2 + \boldsymbol\varepsilon\) with \(\mathbb E\,\boldsymbol\varepsilon = \mathbf 0\) and \(\mathrm{Cov}(\boldsymbol\varepsilon) = \sigma^2\mathbf I\), full column rank, and \(\tilde{\mathbf x}_2 = \mathbf M_1\mathbf x_2\) as in the lecture.

Use the partialling-out theorem to show that \(\hat\beta_2 = \beta_2 + \tilde{\mathbf x}_2^T\boldsymbol\varepsilon / \tilde{\mathbf x}_2^T\tilde{\mathbf x}_2\). Which two facts about \(\mathbf M_1\) do you need?
Find \(\mathbb E\,\hat\beta_2\) and \(\mathrm{Var}(\hat\beta_2)\).
What happens as \(\mathbf x_2\) becomes almost a linear combination of the columns of \(\mathbf X_1\)? Compare two designs with \(\tilde{\mathbf x}_2^T\tilde{\mathbf x}_2 = 100\) and \(\tilde{\mathbf x}_2^T\tilde{\mathbf x}_2 = 4\), with the same \(\sigma^2\).







NoteHint 1






The theorem gives \(\hat\beta_2 = \tilde{\mathbf x}_2^T\mathbf y/\tilde{\mathbf x}_2^T\tilde{\mathbf x}_2\); substitute the model for \(\mathbf y\).










NoteHint 2

title: Week 3 seminar
text:
Before the seminar

The lecture proved one result, the inverse propensity weighting theorem, which you prove again with the slides closed (exercise 4). It stated the optimal threshold theorem and the adjustment theorem and left their proofs to you (exercises 1 and 3), and it stated the confounding gap without deriving it (exercise 2). Do all four on paper before the seminar; the seminar’s problems are variations on them. You may use, without proof, two facts from ST102: the tower property, \(\mathbb E[W] = \mathbb E\big[\mathbb E[W \mid X]\big]\), and that if \(V\) is independent of \(X\), then \(\mathbb E[k(X, V) \mid X = x] = \mathbb E[k(x, V)]\) for any function \(k\) (freeze \(X\) at \(x\); the distribution of \(V\) does not move). A third fact, taking out what is known: \(\mathbb E[f(X)\,W \mid X] = f(X)\,\mathbb E[W \mid X]\). Throughout, assume that every expectation that appears exists: finite means, and finite variances wherever a variance or covariance appears.






WarningHints



Each exercise has hints, collapsed below it. Do not open a hint unless you have been stuck for at least a few minutes, and open them in order. Exercise 4’s proof is on the lecture slides. Solutions to exercises 1 to 3 are shown in the seminar if you ask.


Exercise 1 (optimal threshold theorem). Let \(p(x) = P(Y = 1 \mid X = x)\). A false positive (predict \(1\), truth \(0\)) costs \(c_{FP} \ge 0\), a false negative (predict \(0\), truth \(1\)) costs \(c_{FN} \ge 0\), not both are \(0\), and a correct prediction costs nothing. A rule \(\delta\) assigns a prediction \(\delta(x) \in \{0, 1\}\) to every \(x\).

At a fixed \(x\), write the expected cost of predicting \(1\) and the expected cost of predicting \(0\).
Show that predicting \(1\) has the smaller expected cost exactly when \(p(x) > c^\star = c_{FP}/(c_{FP} + c_{FN})\). What happens at \(p(x) = c^\star\)?
Let \(\delta^\star\) be the rule from (b). Show that \(\mathbb E\big[\text{cost}(\delta^\star(X), Y)\big] \le \mathbb E\big[\text{cost}(\delta(X), Y)\big]\) for every rule \(\delta\).
With equal costs, what is \(c^\star\), and what is the probability of a wrong label at \(x\) under \(\delta^\star\)?







NoteHint 1





Given \(X = x\), \(Y\) is \(1\) with probability \(p(x)\). If you predict \(1\), when is that a mistake, and what does the mistake cost?









NoteHint 2






Compare the two expected costs and solve the inequality for \(p(x)\). “Not both \(0\)” is what lets you divide.










NoteHint 3






Condition on \(X\) first (the tower property), as in week 2’s exercise 1. What do you know about the inner expectation, at every \(x\)?




Exercise 2 (confounding gap). The lecture’s DAG made linear. \(Z\), \(\varepsilon_T\) and \(\varepsilon_Y\) are independent and normal (so that conditioning on \(T = 0\) and on \(T = 1\) makes sense), \(\varepsilon_T\) and \(\varepsilon_Y\) have mean \(0\), \(\mathrm{Var}(T) > 0\), and \[
T = \alpha Z + \varepsilon_T, \qquad Y = \tau T + \beta Z + \varepsilon_Y.
\]

Under \(do(T = t)\), which variables keep their distributions? Show that \(\mathbb E[Y \mid do(T = t)] = \tau t + \beta\, \mathbb E Z\), so that moving \(t\) from \(0\) to \(1\) changes the mean of \(Y\) by \(\tau\).
As observed, show that \(\mathbb E[Y \mid T = t] = \tau t + \beta\, \mathbb E[Z \mid T = t]\), and hence \[
\mathbb E[Y \mid T = 1] - \mathbb E[Y \mid T = 0] = \tau + \beta\,\big(\mathbb E[Z \mid T = 1] - \mathbb E[Z \mid T = 0]\big).
\] Where did you use independence?
Show that the population slope of the least-squares line of \(Y\) on \(T\) alone, \(\mathrm{Cov}(T, Y)/\mathrm{Var}(T)\), is \(\tau + \beta\,\delta\) with \(\delta = \mathrm{Cov}(Z, T)/\mathrm{Var}(T)\). Which quantity in week 2’s omitted-variable bias plays the role of \(\delta\)?
When is the gap zero?







NoteHint 1






Delete \(T\)’s equation and set \(T = t\). Is \(Z\) upstream or downstream of \(T\)?










NoteHint 2






Take \(\mathbb E[\,\cdot \mid T = t]\) of \(Y\)’s equation term by term. \(T\) is a function of \(Z\) and \(\varepsilon_T\); what does that say about \(\varepsilon_Y\) and \(T\)?










NoteHint 3






Expand \(\mathrm{Cov}(T, Y)\) using \(Y\)’s equation. \(\mathrm{Cov}(T, \varepsilon_Y) = 0\) for the reason you found in (b).




Exercise 3 (adjustment theorem). The lecture stated this one; prove it. Structural model: \(Z\), \(\varepsilon_T\) and \(\varepsilon_Y\) independent, \(T = h(Z, \varepsilon_T)\), \(Y = g(T, Z, \varepsilon_Y)\); under \(do(T = t)\) the equation for \(T\) is deleted, \(T\) is set to \(t\), every other equation stays, and the noises keep their distribution. Suppose \(T\) takes finitely many values and \(P(T = t \mid Z) > 0\) with probability one. Show that \[
\mathbb E[Y \mid do(T = t)] = \mathbb E_Z\Big[\,\mathbb E[Y \mid T = t, Z]\,\Big],
\] and say where each assumption is used: the independence of the noises, \(Z\) not being a consequence of \(T\), and the condition on \(P(T = t \mid Z)\).
When \(Z\) takes finitely many values, the formula is commonly written as a sum. The reading writes it this way, for probabilities of \(Y\) rather than its mean, and calls it the adjustment formula. It is the same formula: \[
\mathbb E[Y \mid do(T = t)] = \sum_z \mathbb E[Y \mid T = t, Z = z]\, P(Z = z).
\]
For a continuous \(T\) (as in problem 2 and world D), \(T = t\) exactly has probability \(0\), and the theorem needs two more conditions: \((T, Z)\) has a continuous joint density that is positive everywhere, and \(m_t(z) = \mathbb E[g(t, z, \varepsilon_Y)]\) is continuous in \(t\) and \(z\). Then \(\mathbb E[Y \mid T = t, Z = z]\) is the limit of the average \(Y\) over units with \((T, Z)\) near \((t, z)\), that limit is \(m_t(z)\), and the same proof goes through. The linear normal models in this notebook satisfy both conditions.






NoteHint 1





Start from the intervened world. What is \(Y\) under \(do(T = t)\), and which variables keep their distributions? Give the average over the noise with \(Z\) frozen a name: \(m_t(z) = \mathbb E\big[g(t, z, \varepsilon_Y)\big]\).









NoteHint 2





Use the second ST102 fact, with \(V = \varepsilon_Y\) and \(Z\) in the role of \(X\), to show \(\mathbb E[Y \mid do(T = t)] = \mathbb E_Z\big[m_t(Z)\big]\).









NoteHint 3





Now the observed world: on \(\{T = t, Z = z\}\), \(Y = g(t, z, \varepsilon_Y)\). Why is \(\varepsilon_Y\) independent of \((T, Z)\), and what does that give for \(\mathbb E[Y \mid T = t, Z = z]\)?









NoteHint 4





Why is the distribution of \(Z\) the same in the observed and the intervened worlds?



Exercise 4 (inverse propensity weighting theorem). The lecture proved this one. Close the slides and prove it again. The structural model of exercise 3, with \(T \in \{0, 1\}\) and the propensity score \(\pi(z) = P(T = 1 \mid Z = z)\), where \(0 < \pi(Z) < 1\) with probability one.

Show that \(\mathbb E[Y \mid do(T = 1)] = \mathbb E\big[T\,Y/\pi(Z)\big]\), and say where you used the independence of the noises, \(Z\) not being a consequence of \(T\), and \(\pi(Z) > 0\).
Show that \(\mathbb E[Y \mid do(T = 0)] = \mathbb E\big[(1 - T)\,Y/(1 - \pi(Z))\big]\).
Without the structural model, show by conditioning on \(Z\) that \(\mathbb E\big[T\,Y/\pi(Z)\big] = \mathbb E_Z\big[\,\mathbb E[Y \mid T = 1, Z]\,\big]\). What does that say about the two theorems?







NoteHint 1






Start from what you want. Under \(do(T = 1)\), what is \(Y\), and what is random? To bring \(T\) in, multiply and divide by \(\pi(Z)\).










NoteHint 2






Replace the \(\pi(Z)\) on top by \(\mathbb E_{\varepsilon_T}[T \mid Z, \varepsilon_Y]\). Why are they equal? (The second fact, with \(V = \varepsilon_T\).) Then take the fixed factor inside and use the tower property.










NoteHint 3






At the end, check that \(T\,g(1, Z, \varepsilon_Y) = T\,Y\) when \(T = 0\) and when \(T = 1\).










NoteHint 4






\(T\,Y = Y\,\mathbb 1[T = 1]\), so \(\mathbb E[T\,Y \mid Z] = P(T = 1 \mid Z)\, \mathbb E[Y \mid T = 1, Z]\).

text:
Problems

Problem 1 (costs 5 and 1). A conservation survey classifies penguins from a photograph. Labeling a Chinstrap as an Adelie (a miss) wastes a return visit, cost 5; labeling an Adelie as a Chinstrap (a false alarm) wastes a phone call, cost 1. Write \(p(x) = P(\text{Chinstrap} \mid x)\).

Find the threshold on \(p(x)\) above which predicting Chinstrap has the smaller expected cost. What happens at the threshold itself?
A fitted model gives \(\hat p = 0.25\) for one bird. What does the rule predict, and what would have to be true of \(\hat p\) for that prediction to be the best one at that \(x\)?
The survey hands the same \(\hat p\) to two field teams. For team A a miss costs 5 and a false alarm 1; for team B both cost 1. For which values of \(\hat p\) do the two teams make different calls?
Say in one sentence what the survey decided when it chose 5 and 1.

Problem 2 (the lecture’s DAG, with numbers). Let \(Z\), \(\varepsilon_T\) and \(\varepsilon_Y\) be independent standard normal variables, \(T = Z + \varepsilon_T\) and \(Y = T + 2Z + \varepsilon_Y\).

What is the effect on \(\mathbb E[Y]\) of raising \(t\) by one under \(do(T = t)\)?
Compute \(\mathrm{Var}(T)\), \(\mathrm{Cov}(T, Y)\) and the population slope of the regression of \(Y\) on \(T\) alone, and compare the slope with (a).
Recover the answer to (a) from the distribution of the observed \((T, Z, Y)\) alone. Which result are you using, and where do you need the noises to be independent?

Problem 3 (inverse propensity weighting by hand). \(Z\) is \(0\) or \(1\), each with probability \(\tfrac12\). Treatment depends on \(Z\): \(T = h(Z, \varepsilon_T)\) with \(\pi(0) = 0.2\) and \(\pi(1) = 0.8\). The outcome is \(Y = 2T + 4Z + \varepsilon_Y\), with \(\varepsilon_Y\) of mean \(0\), and \(Z\), \(\varepsilon_T\), \(\varepsilon_Y\) independent.

What is \(\mathbb E[Y \mid do(T = 1)] - \mathbb E[Y \mid do(T = 0)]\)?
Picture 100 units in exactly these proportions. How many are treated with \(Z = 0\), treated with \(Z = 1\), untreated with \(Z = 0\), untreated with \(Z = 1\)? Compute \(\mathbb E[Y \mid T = 1] - \mathbb E[Y \mid T = 0]\) and compare it with (a).
Give each unit the weight that inverse propensity weighting gives it, and multiply each count from (b) by its weight. What do the weighted treated units look like? Compute the inverse propensity weighting estimates of \(\mathbb E[Y \mid do(T = 1)]\) and \(\mathbb E[Y \mid do(T = 0)]\) and compare with (a).
Which units get the largest weights? What would happen to them if \(\pi(0)\) were \(0.01\)?

    Y <- 2 * X + e_y

    Y <- 2.5 * U + e_y
    Z <- NA

    Y <- 2 * e_y
    X <- 0.4 * Y + 0.4 * e_x
    Z <- NA
  } else {                      # D: Z causes both, and X causes Y; Z is observed
    Z <- e_u
    X <- 5 - 2 * Z + e_x
    Y <- 4 + 2 * Z - 3 * X + e_y
  }
  tibble(world = world, X = X, Y = Y, Z = Z, e_u = e_u, e_x = e_x, e_y = e_y)
}

title: Week 4 seminar
text:
Before the seminar

The lecture proved one result, the descent lemma, which you prove again with the slides closed (exercise 1). It stated the ERM form of the bias–variance decomposition and left its two-line proof to you (exercise 2), set the Newton-Raphson exercise on the logistic log-likelihood (exercise 3), and stated no free lunch (exercise 4, a proof on a finite domain). Do all four on paper before the seminar; the seminar’s problems are variations on them. You may use, without proof: the fundamental theorem of calculus along a line, \(f(y) - f(x) = \int_0^1 \nabla f(x + t(y - x))^T (y - x)\, dt\) for a differentiable \(f\); the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality \(|a^T b| \le \|a\|\,\|b\|\); and the tower property, \(\mathbb E[W] = \mathbb E\big[\mathbb E[W \mid X]\big]\). Throughout, assume that every expectation that appears exists.






WarningHints



Each exercise has hints, collapsed below it. Do not open a hint unless you have been stuck for at least a few minutes, and open them in order. Exercise 1’s proof is on the lecture slides. Solutions to exercises 2 to 4 are shown in the seminar if you ask.


Exercise 1 (descent lemma). Let \(f: \mathbb R^p \to \mathbb R\) be differentiable with an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient: \(\|\nabla f(x) - \nabla f(y)\| \le L\,\|x - y\|\) for all \(x, y\), for some \(L > 0\). Fix \(x\), a step size \(\gamma > 0\), and write \(y = x - \gamma\nabla f(x)\) and \(v = y - x\).

Write \(f(y) - f(x)\) as an integral along the segment from \(x\) to \(y\), and split it into \(\nabla f(x)^T v\) plus a remainder.
Bound the remainder by \(\tfrac{L}{2}\|v\|^2\).
Substitute \(v = -\gamma\nabla f(x)\) and show that \(f(y) \le f(x) - \gamma\big(1 - \tfrac12 L\gamma\big)\|\nabla f(x)\|^2\). For which \(\gamma\) is the right-hand side below \(f(x)\), and what does \(\gamma = 1/L\) give?
The lemma says each step decreases \(f\). Give a function with an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient for which the iterates \(x_{t+1} = x_t - \nabla f(x_t)/L\) never converge, and say in one sentence what the lemma does and does not guarantee.







NoteHint 1






Apply the fundamental theorem of calculus along the line to \(f\), with \(x_t = x + tv\). To split, add and subtract \(\nabla f(x)^T v\) inside the integral.










NoteHint 2






Cauchy-Schwarz on \([\nabla f(x_t) - \nabla f(x)]^T v\), then the Lipschitz bound, then \(\|x_t - x\| = t\|v\|\). What is \(\int_0^1 t\, dt\)?










NoteHint 3






Think of a function with no minimum at all. Its gradient is as Lipschitz as you like.




Exercise 2 (bias–variance decomposition, ERM form). Risk \(R(f) = \mathbb E\,\ell(Y, f(X))\). Let \(f^\star\) minimize \(R\) over all predictors, let \(\mathcal F\) be a class of predictors with a best member \(f_{\mathcal F} = \arg\min_{f \in \mathcal F} R(f)\), and let \(\hat f \in \mathcal F\) be the predictor an algorithm returns from the sample (the empirical risk minimizer, or anything else in \(\mathcal F\)).

Show that \(R(\hat f) - R(f_{\mathcal F}) \ge 0\) and \(R(f_{\mathcal F}) - R(f^\star) \ge 0\).
Show that \(R(\hat f) = R(f^\star) + \big[R(\hat f) - R(f_{\mathcal F})\big] + \big[R(f_{\mathcal F}) - R(f^\star)\big]\), and say which term is random and which is fixed once \(\mathcal F\) is chosen.
For squared loss, use week 2’s optimal model theorem to write the approximation term as a squared distance.
The smallest class there is, \(\mathcal F = \{\text{constant functions}\}\), squared loss, \(\hat f = \bar y\) from an i.i.d. sample of size \(n\). Find \(f_{\mathcal F}\), show that the approximation error is \(\mathrm{Var}(f^\star(X))\), and show that the expected estimation error is \(\mathrm{Var}(Y)/n\).







NoteHint 1






What does “\(f_{\mathcal F}\) minimizes \(R\) over \(\mathcal F\)” say about \(R(\hat f)\), given that \(\hat f \in \mathcal F\)?










NoteHint 2






The optimal model theorem: \(R(f) - R(f^\star) = \mathbb E[(f^\star(X) - f(X))^2]\) for every \(f\). Apply it to \(f = f_{\mathcal F}\).










NoteHint 3






For a constant \(c\), \(R(c) = \mathbb E(Y - c)^2 = \mathrm{Var}(Y) + (c - \mathbb E Y)^2\). Then the optimal model theorem once more, and \(\mathrm{Var}(Y) = \mathbb E[\mathrm{Var}(Y \mid X)] + \mathrm{Var}(\mathbb E[Y \mid X])\).




Exercise 3 (score equations, Hessian, Newton-Raphson). Logistic regression with design matrix \(\mathbf X\) (\(n\) rows \(\mathbf x_i^T\)), labels \(y_i \in \{0, 1\}\), and \(p_i(\beta) = 1/(1 + e^{-\mathbf x_i^T\beta})\).

Show that the log-likelihood can be written \(\ell(\beta) = \sum_i \big[y_i\,\mathbf x_i^T\beta - \log(1 + e^{\mathbf x_i^T\beta})\big]\), and that its gradient is \(\nabla\ell(\beta) = \sum_i \mathbf x_i\,(y_i - p_i(\beta)) = \mathbf X^T(\mathbf y - \mathbf p(\beta))\).
Differentiate once more to get the Hessian \(\nabla^2\ell(\beta) = -\sum_i p_i(1 - p_i)\,\mathbf x_i\mathbf x_i^T = -\mathbf X^T\mathbf W\mathbf X\) with \(\mathbf W = \mathrm{diag}(p_i(1 - p_i))\).
Show that \(v^T\nabla^2\ell(\beta)\,v \le 0\) for every \(v\), so \(\ell\) is concave, and say when the inequality is strict for every \(v \ne 0\).
Newton-Raphson finds a root of \(\nabla\ell\) by solving the linear approximation \(\nabla\ell(\beta_t) + \nabla^2\ell(\beta_t)(\beta - \beta_t) = \mathbf 0\) for \(\beta\). Write the update \(\beta_{t+1}\) in terms of \(\mathbf X\), \(\mathbf W_t\), \(\mathbf y\) and \(\mathbf p_t\).







NoteHint 1






\(\log p_i = -\log(1 + e^{-\mathbf x_i^T\beta})\) and \(\log(1 - p_i) = -\mathbf x_i^T\beta - \log(1 + e^{-\mathbf x_i^T\beta})\). For the gradient, \(\tfrac{d}{dz}\log(1 + e^z) = e^z/(1 + e^z)\), which is \(p_i\) at \(z = \mathbf x_i^T\beta\).










NoteHint 2






\(\tfrac{\partial}{\partial\beta} p_i(\beta) = p_i(1 - p_i)\,\mathbf x_i\). (c) \(v^T\mathbf x_i\mathbf x_i^T v = (\mathbf x_i^T v)^2\).




Exercise 4 (no free lunch on a finite domain). A finite set \(\mathcal X\) has \(N\) points. A labeling is a function \(f: \mathcal X \to \{0, 1\}\). A method sees the labels on a fixed training set \(S \subset \mathcal X\) of \(n < N\) points and returns a classifier \(\hat h\), which may be any function of those \(n\) labels. Its error on the points it has not seen is \[
\mathrm{err}(\hat h, f) = \frac{1}{N - n} \sum_{x \notin S} \mathbb 1\big[\hat h(x) \ne f(x)\big].
\]

Draw \(f\) uniformly at random from all \(2^N\) labelings. Show that \(\mathbb E\big[\mathrm{err}(\hat h, f)\big] = \tfrac12\) for every method.
Two methods, \(A\) and \(B\). Suppose \(A\)’s error on the unseen points is smaller than \(B\)’s for some labeling. Show that \(B\)’s is smaller than \(A\)’s for another labeling.
What would have to be true of the world for some method to do better than \(\tfrac12\) on average? Where does that assumption sit in the ERM form of exercise 2?







NoteHint 1





Uniform over all \(2^N\) labelings means that the \(N\) labels \(f(x)\) are independent fair coin flips.









NoteHint 2





Fix \(x \notin S\). \(\hat h(x)\) depends only on the labels on \(S\), and \(f(x)\) is independent of them. Condition on the labels on \(S\): what is \(P\big(\hat h(x) \ne f(x)\big)\)?









NoteHint 3






Average \(\mathrm{err}(\hat h_A, f) - \mathrm{err}(\hat h_B, f)\) over all \(2^N\) labelings.

text:
Problems

Problem 1 (three observations). Three observations, \((x_i, y_i) = (-1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 3)\), a line \(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x\), and the objective \(\hat R_n(\beta) = \tfrac13\sum_i (y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i)^2\).

Compute the gradient of \(\hat R_n\) at \(\beta = (0, 0)\) and take one gradient-descent step with \(\gamma = 0.1\).
At what \(\beta\) does the iteration stop moving, and which equations does that point satisfy?
The curvatures of \(\hat R_n\) are the eigenvalues of \(2\mathbf X^T\mathbf X/n\). Compute them. What is the largest step size for which gradient descent converges from every start, and is \(\gamma = 0.5\) safe?
Which coordinate converges more slowly with \(\gamma = 0.5\), and by what factor does its error shrink per step?

Problem 2 (one direction, then two). One direction with curvature \(a > 0\): \(f(\beta) = \tfrac12 a\beta^2\).

Show that gradient descent with step \(\gamma\) gives \(\beta_t = (1 - \gamma a)^t\beta_0\), and find all \(\gamma\) for which it converges.
Which \(\gamma\) reaches the minimum in one step?
Two directions with curvatures \(10\) and \(1\) and one shared step size. Which \(\gamma\) makes the slower of the two directions shrink fastest, and what is the shrinkage factor per step then?

Problem 3 (a random row). \(\hat R_n(\beta) = \tfrac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \ell_i(\beta)\). Pick an index \(I\) uniformly at random from \(\{1, \dots, n\}\), with the data and \(\beta\) held fixed.

Show that \(\mathbb E_I[\nabla\ell_I(\beta)] = \nabla\hat R_n(\beta)\). Which assumption about where the data came from did you use?
A batch of \(b\) indices drawn independently with replacement, gradient averaged: give its mean and its variance in terms of \(\sigma^2(\beta) = \mathrm{Var}_I[\nabla\ell_I(\beta)]\) (one coordinate at a time is fine).
If the batch is drawn without replacement, is the variance larger or smaller, and what is it when \(b = n\)?
The descent lemma says a full gradient step of size \(1/L\) decreases \(\hat R_n\). Does a step of size \(1/L\) along \(\nabla\ell_I(\beta)\) decrease \(\hat R_n\)? Give a reason or a counterexample.

Problem 4 (the valley with shrinking steps). Gradient descent on the lecture’s valley, \(f(\beta) = \tfrac12(\beta_1^2 + 10\beta_2^2)\), from \(\beta_0 = (-4, 1.2)\) with the step sizes \(\gamma_t = 0.3 \cdot 0.6^t\), \(t = 1, 2, \dots\) (panel C of the lecture).

Show that each coordinate obeys \(\beta_{j, t} = \beta_{j, 0}\prod_{s=1}^t (1 - a_j\gamma_s)\) with \(a_1 = 1\), \(a_2 = 10\).
For the first coordinate, compute the first four factors and say what \(\beta_{1, t}\) converges to (two decimals are enough). Is it the minimizer?
Compute \(\sum_{t \ge 1}\gamma_t\). Which of the two conditions on step sizes from the lecture does this schedule violate, and what does the sum say about how far the iterate can travel?

title: Machine learning
text:
Regularized (i.e. penalized) regression
Motivation: week 4 stopped gradient descent early, and the number of steps became a knob that controlled how far the fit went. Can the knob be written into the objective instead?

For some penalty function \(\mathcal P_\lambda\), which depends on a tuning parameter \(\lambda\), the estimator
\[\hat \beta_\lambda = \arg \min_\beta \| \mathbf y - \mathbf X \beta \|^2_2 + \mathcal P_\lambda(\beta)\] is “regularized” or shrunk (shranken?) toward values that decrease the penalty. Often \(\mathcal P_\lambda = \lambda \| \cdot \|\) for some norm


Many ML methods are optimizing “loss + penalty”

title: Machine learning
text:
Ridge (i.e. L2 penalized) regression

Originally motivated by problems where \(\mathbf X^T \mathbf X\) is uninvertible (or badly conditioned, i.e. almost uninvertible)
If \(p > n\) then this always happens
Least squares estimator is undefined or numerically unstable

For some constant \(\lambda > 0\), \[\text{minimize } \| \mathbf y - \mathbf X \beta \|^2_2 + \lambda \| \beta \|^2\] Shrinks coefficients \(\hat \beta\) toward 0
Larger coefficients are penalized more (squared penalty)

title: Machine learning
text:
What \(\lambda\) controls


Set the gradient of \(\| \mathbf y - \mathbf X \beta \|^2 + \lambda \| \beta \|^2\) to zero (exercise 2): \[
(\mathbf X^T\mathbf X + \lambda I)\,\hat\beta_\lambda = \mathbf X^T\mathbf y
\] \[
\hat\beta_\lambda = (\mathbf X^T\mathbf X + \lambda I)^{-1}\mathbf X^T\mathbf y
\]
\(\mathbf X^T\mathbf X + \lambda I\) is invertible for every \(\lambda > 0\), whatever \(n\) and \(p\): one solution even when \(p > n\)
\(\lambda \to 0\): least squares (when it exists). \(\lambda \to \infty\): \(\hat\beta_\lambda \to \mathbf 0\)










\(\hat\beta_\lambda\) against \(-\log\lambda\): the 16 standardized inputs (eleven numeric, five genre dummies), six named

section: Lasso vs ridge: L1 vs L2 norm penalties
text:
Lasso vs ridge: L1 vs L2 norm penalties
A simple diff to remember lasso/ridge is via the penalty/constraint (1-norm instead of 2-norm). Lasso is
\[\text{minimize } \frac{1}{2n}\| \mathbf y - \mathbf X \beta \|_2^2 \text{ s. t. } \| \beta \|_1 \leq t\] where \(\| \beta \|_1 = \sum_{j=1}^p |\beta_j|\). Lagrangian form
\[\text{minimize } \frac{1}{2n} \| \mathbf y - \mathbf X \beta \|_2^2 + \lambda \| \beta \|_1\]
The lasso often gives estimates with many coefficients set to exactly zero

title: Machine learning
section: A spline is regression on basis functions
text:
A spline is regression on basis functions












A basis: fixed functions \(b_1(x), \ldots, b_J(x)\) of one input, combined by least squares: \[
f(x) = \beta_0 + \sum_{j=1}^J \beta_j\, b_j(x)
\] linear in \(\beta\): ns(gdpPercap, df = J) builds the \(J\) columns for lm()
A natural cubic spline: cubic pieces joined smoothly at knots, linear beyond the ends. The basis functions are the bends the knots allow; lm adds \(\beta_0\)

title: Machine learning
section: The basis size is the knob
text:
The basis size is the knob









Small \(J\): almost a line. Large \(J\): the curve follows the points, and at \(J = n\) it passes through every one (training error zero). Which \(J\)? The selection set, as for \(k\) and \(\lambda\). Later in the course: a penalty on wiggliness instead, with \(J\) as a ceiling

title: Machine learning
text:
Additive modeling assumption

Linearity assumption: each predictor has a coefficient

\[g(\mathbb E[\mathbf y | \mathbf X]) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \mathbf x_1 + \beta_2 \mathbf x_2 + \cdots + \beta_p \mathbf x_p\]

Additivity assumption: each predictor has a function

\[g(\mathbb E[\mathbf y | \mathbf X]) = \beta_0 + f_1( \mathbf x_1) + f_2( \mathbf x_2) + \cdots + f_p(\mathbf x_p)\]
Includes linear models as special case if \(f_j(\mathbf x_j) = \beta_j \mathbf x_j\)
Today each \(f_j\) is a spline with \(J\) basis functions, so the whole model is one least-squares fit on \(pJ\) columns: lm(y ~ ns(x1, J) + ns(x2, J) + ...). The GAM in the reading is this model, with a link

title: Machine learning
text:
A GLM of GLMs
Week 4’s GLM: the inverse link applied to a linear predictor, \(g^{-1}(\mathbf x^T\beta)\). Now iterate it












Each hidden unit has the form of a logistic regression of the inputs, with its own weights: \(h_k(x) = g^{-1}(w_{k0} + w_k^T x)\), with \(g\) the logit link, \(g^{-1}(z) = 1/(1 + e^{-z})\)
The output is a linear regression on the hidden units (logistic, for a label): \(f(x) = \beta_0 + \sum_{k=1}^M \beta_k\, h_k(x)\)
A GLM whose inputs are the outputs of \(M\) GLMs. Iterate once more: a deep network

A basis like part 3’s, except that the basis is fitted to the data along with the coefficients, and each \(h_k\) uses every input at once

How it is fitted. All \(M(p + 1) + M + 1\) weights at once, by gradient-based optimization (week 4) on a loss with every feature of week 4’s part 3: not one valley but many, with plateaus and saddles between them. Today’s fits use nnet(), which runs a quasi-Newton method
The knob. \(M\), the number of hidden units, chosen on the selection tracks like the others; depth and a penalty on the weights are later knobs. In R, nnet(size = M, linout = TRUE)

title: Machine learning
text:
Four dimensions, not one









Axis
The question about \(f^\star\)
Who bets which way




wide or tall
how \(p\) compares with \(n\)
least squares needs full column rank for one fit; the additive fit and a network overfit when \(n\) is small; ridge and the lasso fit at any \(p\)


sparse or dense
how many inputs matter
the lasso bets few; least squares and ridge spread the fit over all; a forest tolerates idle inputs, \(k\)-NN pays for them


smooth or discontinuous
how \(f^\star\) moves with each input
splines, \(k\)-NN and networks bet smooth; trees bet on steps


additive or interactive
whether inputs act separately
the additive fit bets separately; trees, forests, \(k\)-NN and networks allow interactions




Four separate questions, not one scale from simple to complex. A family is a bet on the answers; a selection set says which bet paid

Week 1’s curse: \(k\)-NN near the bottom on every truth, seven idle inputs. Week 4’s no free lunch: no family won every truth, and none can.

title: Machine learning
text:
What the training error hides
On most rows of the leaderboards the training MSE sat below the test or selection MSE, the forest’s by a factor of four on the truths and of six on Spotify; on a few rows it sat above. Luck, or a law, and what are the exceptions?
Training data \((x_i, y_i)\), \(i = 1, \ldots, n\), independent draws from the population; a class \(\mathcal F\) fixed before the data (the planes; the spline fits with a given basis); \(f_{\mathcal F}\) the best in \(\mathcal F\), the minimizer of \(R\) over it; \(\hat f\) the empirical risk minimizer, the minimizer of \(\hat R_n\) over \(\mathcal F\) (week 4)

Three numbers: \(\mathbb E[\hat R_n(\hat f)]\), \(R(f_{\mathcal F})\), \(\mathbb E[R(\hat f)]\). Put them in order, and write down what you used to do it.

title: Machine learning
text:
Optimism theorem
A function fixed before the data has an unbiased training error; \(\hat f\) was chosen to make its own small, and cannot beat \(f_{\mathcal F}\) on the population
Training data i.i.d.; \(\mathcal F\) fixed before the data; \(\hat f\) the empirical risk minimizer over \(\mathcal F\); \(f_{\mathcal F}\) the best in \(\mathcal F\) (risks finite, minimizers exist). Then \[
\mathbb E\big[\hat R_n(\hat f)\big] \;\le\; R(f_{\mathcal F}) \;\le\; \mathbb E\big[R(\hat f)\big]
\]

Training error flatters the model: on average it sits below the best risk the class can reach, and the fitted model’s risk above it. A test set estimates \(R(\hat f)\); its average is the right end.

Proof: exercise 1. Covers least squares, a fixed spline basis, ridge and lasso with a fixed radius; not a fixed \(\lambda\), a tree, a forest, \(k\)-NN, or a knob chosen on the data

Each family is a bet on the shape of \(f^\star\)

title: Palmer penguins
text:
Provenance and license
Gorman, Williams and Fraser (2014), Palmer Station Long Term Ecological Research program; packaged by Horst, Hill and Gorman as palmerpenguins. The R package and its data are CC0.


R access
palmerpenguins::penguins. Use the qualified name: modeldata also exports a penguins (7 columns, no year) and masks it when attached later.


Unit of observation
A penguin (344 rows), 8 columns: species, island, bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm, flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g, sex, year.


Target and loss
Week 3: species, Adelie against Chinstrap (219 birds after dropping incomplete measurements), 0–1 loss or a cost-weighted loss with the costs stated.


Available at prediction time
The measurements and island, sex, year. In this dataset island completely separates Chinstrap from Gentoo (Chinstraps are on Dream, Gentoos on Biscoe; Adelies occur on all three islands), so a model with island in it is solving a different, easier task; say so if a student uses it.


Permitted predictors
Week 3: bill_length_mm and bill_depth_mm (the default), flipper_length_mm alone (the weak model for the ROC curve).


Missingness
Two birds lack all four measurements; eleven lack sex. drop_na() on the columns used.


Split unit and seed
Birds. Week 3 fits on all 219 birds with no split: the point is the mechanism, and every number in the seminar is computed on the training rows (apparent performance; the validation week says what that flatters).


Baseline
Predict the majority class, Adelie (the seminar computes its accuracy).


Complication it carries
None social. Near-separability on the bill measurements: glm warns about fitted probabilities of 0 or 1, a live example of the lecture’s “too easy” slide.


Limitations
Three islands, three seasons, one research program: a clean dataset with no deployment story, which is why it is used when the mechanism is the lesson.


Fictional?
No.
